utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would you please call the case, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-04-74-PT, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm now turning to the Prosecution for appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Ken Scott for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ken Scott for the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Daryl Mundis for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'AOUST
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Josee D'Aoust for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: I have a technical problem, please. [Interpretation] I can't hear the interpretation. Very well. I'm now turning to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Michael Karnavas for Dr. Prlic; and with me is Suzana Tomanovic, co-counsel for Dr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, I'm co-counsel for Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Vesna Alaburic, Defence counsel for Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Tomislav Jonjic, Defence counsel for the accused Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. For the Defence of Mr. Berislav Pusic, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and my legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me greet all the people present in the courtroom: The Prosecution, the Defence counsel, Mr. Praljak, too. I guess he's in Zagreb. I hope we soon can see him. Yes, we can see him in the picture. I also have a problem with interpretation. I'd like somebody to come over and check. For the technical booth, apparently the volume is not high enough. Very well. We can proceed. As you know, this Status Conference has been convened for two reasons: On the one hand, we want to take stock of the pre-trial procedure, and we also want to settle a few problems in view of opening this trial. As you know, I have a draft agenda for the beginning of the trial proceedings. If all goes well, we should start on the 25th of April, it's being understood that on the day before, on the 24th, we would have a Pre-Trial Conference. In other words, by that date, the Prosecution will have to comply with obligations expressed in a previous order. They have to provide us with charts and lists so that the Trial Chamber and the Defence counsel can cross-reference the 9.500 exhibits disclosed to the Defence and the 400 Prosecution witnesses. To date, I am not able at all to know which exhibit is going to be introduced through which witness. As you know, Rule 90 is very specific. It provides that the Chamber must control the proceedings, see how the witness is going to testify, and -- so exercise the control over the mode of interrogating witnesses and presenting evidence so as to make the interrogation presentation effective for the ascertainment of the truth and to avoid needless consumption of time. And as a Pre-Trial Judge, as I told you already, once I believe that the case is trial ready, I must report to the other two Judges of the Trial Chamber, pass the full file on to them. And this can only be done if I am in a position to tell the Judges how long the trial is likely to last, what the witnesses are going to be doing in relation to the charges in the indictment, and to check whether there are not too many witnesses or too many exhibits. In order to do so, very quickly I must receive from the Prosecution the information requested. So this is not a small case where you have accused pleading guilty that should be wrapped up in a matter of two or three months. Here we have six accused, they all plead not guilty, and as I said, we have 9.500 exhibits and a forecast of 400 witnesses. If you add onto this and looking at previous cases, the Hadzihasanovic-Kubura case, for instance, if the Defence were to provide as many documents as the Prosecution, or even more, we would be in peaks like the Himalayas when it comes to deducing evidence. Equally, if the Prosecution were -- the Defence were to call as many witnesses as the Prosecution, we would have hundreds of witnesses. In addition to this, if I think back of a trial currently happening, the Slobodan Milosevic, from what I read last week, to date 400 witnesses were heard and some 1.250 Prosecution exhibits were tendered, including 200 video clips, and that trial has been going on for five years. So if we take this as a yardstick as well as the Hadzihasanovic-Kubura case, and given our current forecasts - I want to avoid any misunderstanding - I can tell you that at a minimum this trial is going to take at least four years, not taking into account possible interruptions because of illness or other reasons, because that, too, can cause delay. So in order to see clearly, I really absolutely need to know the following: How are the 9.500 exhibits going to be processed? How are they going to be broken down, witness by witness? But first of all, I must remind everybody, as this had been done by the Blagojevic Chamber in a decision on the admissibility of evidence, the following had been said, and I fully share their view. Pursuant to the Statute, this Tribunal has as a mission to create conditions that may create peace in the former Yugoslavia. In a decision of January 2003 it had been said that there is no peace without justice, and to have justice, you have to have truth, and you have to establish truth, and this can only be done once witnesses have been heard and once evidence has been produced. In respect of evidence, 9.500 documents, that is, in order to help you clarify matters, next week I shall issue a decision. This has been done by many Chambers, including the Blagojevic Chamber, regarding the test or criteria for the admissibility of evidence. So in a nutshell, I'm going to tell you - you know that, of course, but I think it's worth reminding ourselves - of these criteria. You know that our Rules of Procedure and Evidence is a very wise and sophisticated mix of common law and civil law. With regard to evidence, the Judges of this Tribunal do not have to look into evidence just on the basis of Australian law or American law or German law. We must be based on the Rules, because this is our main reference tool. So with this as a starting point, when you look into the Rules themselves, you can see that they're very flexible. In the letter and in the spirit of the Rules it is rather easy to have evidence admitted, but of course there are certain conditions to be fulfilled. Both Prosecution and Defence must keep the following in mind: The mere fact that a document is admitted as evidence during the trial proceedings does not mean that the evidence is reliable, relevant, and has probative value. These elements can only be determined at the end of the trial proceedings. It can very well be that evidence introduced through a witness in the courtroom is not very reliable or not at all prima facie, but if you think that it is hardly reliable but one, two, three years down the track it can be altogether different. So the fate of this evidence is determined when the Judges discuss the case at the end of the trial. Only then is the relevance and is the probative value determined, and this is scrutinised, of course, in the light of the parties' contributions to assessing the evidence through the examination-in-chief, through cross-examination, or through filings or through the final briefs. Therefore -- so there can only be opposition to a piece of evidence being tendered only if there is some real doubt as to the authenticity of the said evidence. If the Prosecution tenders this, of course the Defence can say, well, objection as to the authenticity, and of course the Trial Chamber will look into the issue. As to the reliability, do not confuse authenticity and reliability. These are two different matters. The reliability is the contents of the document. What can be said as to a given fact or as to reliability of an individual? Reliability can come out in the examination-in-chief, in cross-examination, or in the witness statements as such, and through the system we can have an idea of the indicia of reliability. But even at this stage of the proceedings we are not very sure, but in the Prosecution's or the Defence's strategy, if the evidence is being tendered it means that the one asking for it to be tendered believes that there are other elements that are going to support this very piece of evidence. On the other hand, do not forget that when an exhibit is given a number, if later on it turns out that it is not an authentic exhibit, if it -- if problems arise, the Trial Chamber, upon request by the parties, can exclude the exhibit. You know how it works. And also there is this other Rule of the preponderance of evidence. You know it very well, so no need to dwell on it. This being said, this is my goal. This is going to be a megatrial, a multiple accused trial. I can't see Mr. Praljak any more.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It is "the best evidence rule" instead of "preponderance of evidence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, here he is again. So in order not to waste time, we must develop a system in such a manner that the -- if you have a witness in the courtroom, if there is evidence to be tendered, there should not be any objections, or if there are any, they should only be based on the issue of authenticity, because if we start having discussions on the authenticity of exhibits, that means that the trial's going to be paralysed. So the mechanism we need to evolve is as follows: We've got the 9.500 documents, and they've been classified by date, origin, source. Of course we still haven't got the witnesses. I hope that by then we will receive from the Prosecution the witness list matching the exhibit list. So we've got 9.500 documents, and they could already now be given numbers for identification purposes. So we could have numbers from 1 to 9.499. Thereafter, when we have the witnesses in the courtroom, the Prosecution will submit to the witness and the Judges of the Trial Chamber a folder, a binder, containing the documents to be adduced because the witness is here in the courtroom and is in a position to provide information on the said documents, because they have authored the documents or because they had knowledge of the documents at the time. This means that once the witness has finished his or her testimony, the documents will be given final numbers. And this also, of course, will apply to the Defence when comes the time of the Defence case. So starting from this, we have another problem that arises; the e-court problem, or system. I guess you have been trained or initiated into this system. Soon I'm going to issue an order on this. We're going to have a specific hearing devoted to the e-court system so that the Registry can come and tell everybody how a hearing can take place with the e-court system. You know, it's highly sophisticated technology, and it can make us save a lot of time during trial, but I personally believe that there is a shortcoming with this system. The documents that are going to be admitted into evidence have been scanned, will have received numbers, but as a Judge, I need, when a document is presented to a witness, I need to see, to feel, touch the document and compare it with other documents, and this cannot happen when I'm looking at you, when I'm listening, when I look at the transcript, and when I'm still using my computer. It can't be done. But whilst I'm leafing through documents in a binder, I can very well look at you and listen to you. So I know that the Prosecution is used to doing this. It has done so in previous cases when we have witnesses. The Prosecution is going to have an exhibit list in relation to the specific witness. This brings me to another issue. Presently I do not want the Prosecution to operate in the following manner: You have a witness in the courtroom. He or she is being submitted a document or two, and then a few months later we have a filing for the admission of documents that could have been submitted to the witness when he or she was in court. In other words - and this is a very common law type of proceeding - documents must be submitted when the witness is in court. Personally, I would find it very difficult to admit documents without any discussion around it or around them, and discussions can only take place when the witness concerned is in court. I'm looking at Mr. Mundis while saying so. He knows perfectly well what I'm thinking of, because we have had previous examples of this type of procedure by the Prosecution. A witness must be submitted all the exhibits to be tendered. Of course such exhibits will be cross-examined, and the Defence will, in turn, produce evidence to support their case during cross-examination. It shows how important Defence counsel are. They play a major part. And this was settled yesterday. Mr. Praljak must know this already. Yesterday, we made a decision, asking the Registrar, in the interests of justice, to assign counsel to Mr. Praljak. So in the next few days Mr. Praljak will be assigned counsel. I'm sure he will be pleased by this decision, but there's another side to the decision. There is an annex in which Mr. Praljak is asked to answer a number of questions. So once Mr. Praljak is given the decision, he will have to answer the questions put by the Chamber so we will be able to move ahead much faster. In the pre-trial stage now, this issue of counsel is settled. So at our next meeting, we'll have a new lawyer representing Mr. Praljak. At this juncture, before going on with the agenda, let me speak to the pending requests before dealing with the so-called technical issues. First of all, the reminder: We issued a decision yesterday regarding Mr. Praljak's counsel. I've just said so. On the 3rd of February, we denied the Prosecution request for judicial notice pursuant to Rule 94(A) and 89(C). On the 9th of February, we also denied the Prosecution request dated 26th of January, 2006, for admission of evidence by ECMM. So you will have understood straight away that since these requests were denied, there's no point in putting or in filing new motions or requests. They could have the same fate. Now, you have this chart or witness and exhibit lists. I've mentioned this before. It might be that the Prosecution will want to give me an answer later, but I just point out now that as a Pre-Trial Judge, I have asked a similar list in the Dragomir Milosevic case, and in that case the OTP largely met my request. They used the Excel software to do so whilst you here say it's not possible to do so. Pending requests. There's one filed on the 4th of April, 2005 regarding judicial notice pursuant to Rule 94(B). Soon you will have a decision on this. There is a Prosecution request asking the Defence to possibly notify the use of the alibi special defence but that may be a motion regarding the difference. There are four confidential motions regarding Rule 92 bis (A), (B), (C) and (D). You will soon have a decision. They will probably be joined into one single motion with one decision. Then we have a September 2005 motion regarding the suppression of a witness statement. Yesterday I prepared a draft decision. Therefore, you should have the decision very soon. There's also a motion for the production of documents. It's addressed to Croatia. That shouldn't raise too many problems. There is another motion for admission of UNPROFOR documents from the Spanish Battalion. Here, too, you'll soon have a decision, all the more since a Spanish Battalion witness will make it possible to settle this issue very soon. Then we have a motion by Mr. Praljak regarding translation problems for documents, but within a few days he should have a Defence counsel, so this will be moot. So this is regarding pending motions. I'm trying to speed up the decision-making process so that they should be all settled by the 24th of April. But you know I issue a decision on a daily basis. This represents a lot of work. Before giving the floor to the Prosecution, I believe I should provide you a number of information you probably have already about the preparation of the trial regarding the Judges, regarding the assistants who will be helping the Chamber during the trial and who have been assigned to us by the Registrar. As for the Judges, I've already said so before, I will be the Presiding Judge in this case, and I will be assisted by two Ad Litem Judges who will be appointed by the UN Secretary-General two weeks before the commencement of the trial. These two Judges will have two weeks to familiarise themselves with the main exhibits, with the main materials in this case. That means that we will find out, all of us, the identity of these Judges around the 10th of April. There is also something that is pending that has not been resolved yet. That is the question of whether we should have an additional Ad Litem Judge. Therefore, if a Judge was to disappear during the trial - that's happened before, unfortunately - or if a Judge is taken ill, then the trial will be able to go ahead. At the moment, this is under discussion in New York, but if there was to be a fourth Judge, then there would be the -- the issue raised would be that of the amendment of the Rules, because that is not provided for by the Rules. A lot of things are provided for by the Rules, but not that case where you have an additional Judge in a Trial Chamber. But this could be done very quickly. And then -- but if we have the additional Judge, there would be other questions that would have to be solved. Will the Judge -- would the Judge have to be there during the full four years of the trial or just in case he or she is needed or just at the beginning of the Prosecution case, at the time when the 98 bis motions are considered or -- and at the end. These are all questions that will have to be solved, answered, if that Judge, if that fourth Judge is appointed. But I can't tell you any more. I know the issue was raised in New York, but we have not had any feedback from New York yet. Now, as for the staff assisting the Trial Chamber, at the moment I only have with me the legal officer, who is sitting before me, and the assistant, who is sitting to my right, as well as a P4 assistant; and the team of assistants will be -- receiving new members in the next few days, I hope. In any case, I addressed the Registrar about that issue myself, because you can perfectly understand, all of you here, that when you have a case where the accused pleads guilty and the case takes four months, you need at least four assistants. But here are we in a case of a completely different magnitude, and we need very much higher number of assistants than in a regular case. But as of today, I do -- haven't received any feedback about that particular issue. But in any case, let me tell you that if I do not have at my disposal the necessary team to face with all the work entailed by the trial, I will then be forced to seize the Bureau of the matter, stating that I cannot preside over such a trial if I do not have the necessary human resources. But in that particular matter as well, I am expecting the leadership of the Tribunal to be aware of that particular problem. I know that, as for the Registrar, he is very aware that the outcome of the trial is vital for the completion strategy, for us to finish the mandate of the Tribunal before 2010. But I hope that in the very near future I will be informed about the resources that will be provided to the Chamber, and I will immediately inform you about that, because I know that your work depends also on the response the Judges can give to your motions. Let me just give you an example. When you have one accused with one Defence counsel, and if there is a motion, then there can be a response immediately, but when you have six accused, several motions, responses, et cetera, then that's a lot of work. And in order to face that workload, you need to have the necessary resources. But I'm very hopeful. I'm very hopeful that the necessary resources will be provided to the Chamber in order to allow us to begin in the best possible conditions. For the past three months, I have been working almost 24 hours a day on this case, almost, although at the same time I have to work on a judgement that will be issued very shortly. But you have to be aware that I am dealing very closely with this particular case in order to allow the Prosecution and the Defence to start the trial in the best possible conditions. And as for the commencement of -- and as for this trial, I mentioned earlier on that it is a trial that is likely to last a few years. And on that issue, I would like to remind you all of the following, and I'd like to have your reaction on that point as well: As you know, it's likely that we will sit on that case for a few years. That's a fact. Considering that fact, is it reasonable to have five-day sittings, from Monday to Friday without any interruptions? Whereas this case, because of the number of witnesses and exhibits involved, this case requires a lot of work upstream and downstream by the parties. If we sit from Monday to Friday, will the Defence be in a position to meet with the accused in order to take stock of the situation, to consider and -- to consider the cross-examinations, the Defence case, et cetera? Under such circumstances, would it not be a good idea to consider a trial schedule that would allow the Defence and the Prosecution two or three days to -- of preparation at the end of the week? In that spirit, I would consider the following schedule: We could begin on Monday afternoon each week, have a hearing on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. Four hearings a day -- a week, in other words, to allow the Defence to -- preparation time on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, in order to start work again on the following week, and so on. If the trial was to last only three or four months, then a five-day working week would be perfectly acceptable, but we're looking at a trial that is probably going to last a few years, so then it's completely different. And when you compare the situation of this case with other cases, for example Baghdad with the Saddam Hussein trial, you see that in that particular case there are a few days of hearing in the courtroom and then an interruption for a few weeks. In some jurisdictions, hearings are held for a few days, one, two, or three days, and then followed by a break of a week or so. I've had that experience myself of five days of hearing in a row, and it can be quite exhausting for all parties involved. These are a few comments I wanted to share with you to get your reaction on that point, because I would be -- I would like to have your position on that particular point, particularly from the Defence counsel, who of course have to work on the defence, on the preparation of the defence of their respective clients. But before covering the remaining items on the agenda, I would like to turn to the Prosecution and ask the representatives of the Prosecution where they stand currently in terms of these charts, of the preparation of the charts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, Your Honour, we have stated our position repeatedly, as you know, both in writing and orally, expressing our views on this topic and the great deal of time and effort that is involved in preparing these charts, which have not previously been required in any case that we're aware of, and we are -- all I can say now is that we are engaged in very intense and extensive efforts to prepare these charts and proceeding to complete them as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This leads me to the following observations: Let me give you a background about the confirmation of this case, because I was the Confirming Judge in this case. One day, as the Confirming Judge, I received your request for confirming the indictment, and I received about two square metres of -- worth of documents. I did not measure all these documents precisely, but I was faced with a mountain of documents. I myself, with the help of my assistant, made a prima facie verification, trying to verify whether what was stated in the indictment was justified by documents provided by you. So there was a verification conducted using this mountain of documents that had been given to us. Following that process, the indictment was confirmed. But when the Prosecution provided us with that mountain of documents, I tend to think that the Prosecution already had an idea about the names of the witnesses who are going to testify in the case and their nexus with the exhibits, the material. Last time, the Defence reminded us that the Prosecution has been preparing this case for the past eight years. If after eight years you're not in a position to tell us today which exhibit, which document will be put to each witness, this raises a major -- a fundamental issue. If we look at the indictment and the pre-trial brief, which is a rehash of the indictment, in this pre-trial brief we had information about the way the evidence was going to put forward, and it is my duty to check that. You have planned to deal with the issue of the joint criminal enterprise. That's what I can read at paragraph 17 of the indictment. The joint criminal enterprise, you will have to establish it, you will have to demonstrate that there was a joint criminal enterprise. In order to do so, you will have to call witnesses, and you have to use documents, because before coming criminal, a common enterprise can be of a political nature, and it only becomes a criminal enterprise once a number of crimes have been committed. Therefore, you must know what witnesses will come to demonstrate the existence of this joint criminal enterprise, all the more so since, from what I understand, that's where you want to start the trial. In the second part of the pre-trial brief and of the indictment, you deal with the liability of each accused under Article 7(1) of the Statute, based on the joint criminal enterprise theory. In the indictment, the Article 7(3) is also mentioned. It is stated in the indictment that the accused are liable under Article 7(1) and/or Article 7(3). Therefore, Article 7(3) is mentioned in the indictment. As you know, there is case law that has been developed around Article 7(3); effective control on clearly identified subordinate units. You also have the idea of knowledge, the concept of reasonable measures that might have been taken to prevent or to stop actions, and there's also the concept of punishment, penalties. And when I read the pre-trial brief, I do not find much on that subject. In my order, I had asked the Prosecution to prepare, take charts, taking into account Article 7(1) and 7(3), but for the time being I have not received any information about that. Yesterday, I read the response to the pre-trial brief by one of the accused, and in at that response it was stated that the accused was not in a position to know exactly what he was charged with. Furthermore, if I read your submissions, I find that, according to what you say, the joint criminal enterprise involved a number of persons who are dead today. Thus, I do not know whether as part of your evidence you will introduce evidence to show or to establish that these people who are dead today were part of the joint criminal enterprise. In any case, they -- they are mentioned in the indictment. I also read that three persons - Kordic, Naletelic, and Blaskic - three people who were convicted, were part of this joint criminal enterprise. And yesterday, I found out that Blaskic and Kordic were not charged with joint criminal enterprise counts. I read that with great interest yesterday. Therefore, it's all the more important for us to be able to receive as quickly as possible this cross-reference between the exhibits and between witnesses, because at the moment what we have is witnesses that you have cross-referenced with the various paragraphs of the indictment. This will only make sense when we have the cross-reference with the exhibits, because from what I understand from your case -- but what I'm saying is also in the interests of the Judges and in the interests of the Defence; we all need to know where we are going, and in order to know where we are going, we need to have a clear idea about the Prosecution case, about what you want to establish. From what I understand, you are trying to establish there was a joint criminal enterprise, then you want to move on to the individual liabilities of each accused, and then you want to move on to the point of the acts and crimes committed in each municipality. That's what you mentioned yesterday. It's a very interesting plan of action, and that's very understandable, but in order for us to work with that, the Defence has to be in a position to cross-examine the witnesses, and the Judges should not be confused with all the ten thousands of documents you want to tender. So we need to know what documents are going to be tendered for each witness, for what purpose. That's why I'd like to turn to you again to tell you that it's absolutely vital for us to know to which witness what exhibit is related and for what purpose, to demonstrate what. So what can the Prosecution tell me about this? And then afterwards I will give the floor to the Defence, because I'm sure that Defence counsel have a number of comments to make about this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can only say what we've said before in our filings and orally. That is that the charts that Your Honour has asked us to prepare are not required by Rule 65 ter and other Rules. They were not required by the previous Trial Chamber, previous Pre-Trial Judge. The Chamber has imposed a very large and considerable burden on the Prosecution to prepare these particular charts, and it should not come as any surprise to anyone that they will take very considerable time and effort to prepare. It is an entirely false argument and a false position for anyone to suggest that the Prosecution is not prepared to go to trial, because we have repeatedly stated that we are prepared, and we stated so in our filing on the 30th of January, 2006. However, if the Pre-Trial Judge wishes to impose new and additional requirements, then in all respect to the Judge, you have to allow us sufficient time to prepare those documents. They were not prepared before and they were never required before. So all I can say, Your Honour, is that the Prosecution is engaged in intense efforts, in extensive efforts to prepare the material as soon as we possibly can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I take good note of the fact of what you've just said, and I'm going to give the floor to the Defence counsel later, but let me try to assist you here. I had a look at the crimes committed in the Capljina municipality, and when I read your submissions, I find that a number of events took place on the 10th of May, 1993; on the 20th of April, 1993; on the 13th of July, 1993; from the 13th of -- to the 15th of July, 1993; on the 11th of August; and then events took place between the 27th and the 5th of August, 1993; and then other events in August and September in that municipality. In other words, based on these, these -- or during these periods, at these dates, a number of events took place. Let me just take three of them. There was a case of wilful killing, or murder, of an 83-year-old person. Twelve people disappeared in Brdo, and two women are alleged to have been killed in Kevcici. So if we just take these specific events, within 15 to 20 minutes, based on the list of exhibits - and I can do that myself - you should be in a position to tell us what exhibits will be used to demonstrate that an 80-year-old person was killed in Kevcici. If we stay in the same municipality, we see that three mosques were destroyed there: The Oplicici mosque in Lokve, and the one located in Visici. That's what we can read in your submissions. Three mosques were destroyed. But that's not enough. You have to prove that these mosques were indeed destroyed. How can you prove? Through witnesses or through documents. So you have to look through your documents, any reference to these three mosques, but I don't think that such an exercise will take weeks. And I can give you further examples. If you do not conduct that exercise, if you do not do that work, I will have to do it instead of you. In other words, you're asking the Judge to do what it is your duty to do, to do your work for you. I would now like to give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, good morning. First let me just touch upon this last issue. I believe the Prosecution is in error when it states that never before has it been required to provide the sort of charts that has been requested by this particular Chamber. It is my understanding that in the Stakic case and in the Blagojevic case both Trial Chambers requested what they called proofing charts. Judge Schomburg began that tradition. It was very useful, because again it assists everyone, including the Defence, but also, more importantly, the Trial Chamber, because unlike in the civil tradition, there is no dossier, and of course the Trial Chamber is entitled to be prepared because they have certain mandates, one of which is questioning witnesses if they feel it necessary. So I believe there has been a procedure set in place, one that was used in the past, one that the Prosecution was aware of, one that should have been done by the Prosecution irrespective of the Trial Chamber's order, because I think, in a case of this magnitude, it is humanly impossible to sift through the 9.000 plus exhibits, or whatever the number is, and try to figure out what it is they're trying to prove. What compounds the situation is the fact -- is the way the indictment has been drafted, which in my opinion is done so in a very American approach, and I say that having practised in the United States where the tradition is to charge everything that is virtually within the Statute so nothing is left out in case the jury may come back and find one scrap of evidence to convict on something. The Trial Chamber quite rightly pointed out the Rules of Evidence that are applied in this Court which are of a much more flexible nature, one that is primarily based on the civil law system and one that makes complete sense. Keeping that in mind, however, doesn't mean that the Defence should put in a position where it literally has to try to find the needle in the haystack. Preparing a case of this magnitude for the Defence is virtually -- it's made virtually impossible by the way the indictment is drafted. They have -- if you go through it carefully, and when you sit down and you try to have a discussion with the Prosecution at the 65 ter meetings, it is quite obvious that it is not just the charges themselves but it's everything that's contained within the four corners of those documents called the indictment, that the Prosecution wishes to use at some point or another, be it -- be it what they call background information or what have you, they want to use anything that they possibly can so that at the end of the trial they can argue that, one, that the Defence had sufficient notice; and two, if it was stated in the indictment and it wasn't challenged, you can accept it and make it part -- or factor it into your conclusions at the end of the trial. I think the Trial Chamber is correct in pointing out that when, as I believe I understand the Trial Chamber's concern, was when the indictment comes forward to be confirmed, in essence if you are being provided with about two metres of documents, that in and of itself would give an indication that, one, the Prosecution should be at that point in time prepared to go to trial; and two, they would at least know what their case is. I always like to say, when I teach trial advocacy, you have to know your destination in order to get there. But we have, however -- the tradition, unfortunately, in this Tribunal has emerged is one where you can indict and then, as the years go by, continue to investigate and hope and pray that somehow you will find evidence that will support something that you have alleged in the indictment because you are alleging everything, God forbid something you should miss and somebody might be acquitted. I think that's the approach they have taken. So as -- here we are, and rightly so, Your Honour, you pointed out that eight years or so they have been working on these cases, because they have been building it up. You're also right in noting that in the previous cases, Blaskic, Kordic, Naletelic and Martinovic, joint criminal enterprise, they were never claimed to have been members of the joint criminal enterprise yet today we find that they are included in that and the Prosecution wishes to use those judgements as a basis of forming adjudicated facts and agreed facts and also to bring in all sorts of testimony and documents uncorroborated in this particular trial, and we find that objectionable. Why? If you look at -- and I've mentioned this before in some of the 65 ter meetings: If you look at what was alleged in those cases and if you, for instance, approach it from a very continental approach, you're going to only direct your defence based on what you're being charged. So if they're bringing in concepts such as whether there was an international armed conflict or whether there was -- what the structure of the HVO government was, or Herceg-Bosna was, and those are not part of the charges that a Defence has to attack in order to represent his client, much of that goes unchallenged and now we find ourselves in the situation where the Prosecution is trying to bring it in as already-establish facts and therefore they don't need to prove it. I don't want to go on, and I certainly want to stay on point. The point is this: It's becoming increasingly impossible to prepare this case and to provide our clients, particularly my client, a reasonable degree of effective assistance of counsel. I think he deserves that. The Prosecutor Madam Del Ponte goes around the world preaching about how countries, certain countries, including Croatia being one of them, need to comply with the Tribunal, and I think that is her duty and that's her obligation, and I commend her for that. But at the same time it should be noted that when an accused comes over here, when a country either brings somebody over here or an individual volunteers, as all of these individuals volunteered to come here upon learning they were indicted, once they come here, the Prosecution is entitled to treat them with fairness and dignity and to make sure their rights are being protected. And I think that obligation also extends to the Registry as well to making sure that those accused have the sufficient funds and resources to adequately prepare their cases. Equality of arms doesn't just mean just adequacy of resources. It also means when we come into court, it should be a level playing field, and we cannot have a level playing field if I'm trying to figure out what exactly the Prosecution is attempting to prove in his or her case because of the way the indictment has been constructed and because of the way the evidence is coming in. I understand that Mr. Scott is being asked to do something at this point in time which perhaps will take a great deal of energy, effort, and coordination within his team. That -- however, what I -- I must say, and I say this with all due respect and with a little bit of sadness, that what I'm hearing is some resistance from that aisle. I sense that somehow they feel that if they provide the Defence with adequate notice, not just through the indictment but also in the way they present their case, in the way they document their evidence, in the way they present the proofing charts which assist the Chamber, that somehow they will lose some sort of a disadvantage, and unfortunately that is what I call -- that's what I say that almost the worst of the American habits that we find in our own legal system has creeped into this particular Tribunal and that it has become a game. It has become such an adversarial game that first and foremost it becomes a winners gain all. It's all about winning and not necessarily providing the Defence with an opportunity to test their evidence and of course assist the Trial Chamber in arriving at the truth. And as I said, I can go on and on, but I share all of your frustrations, and frankly, I'm heartened by the fact that what I'm hearing from the Trial Chamber that you are really, truly interested in providing us with a fair opportunity to test the evidence and for us to present our cases and we cannot do so unless we do have this continuing pressure put upon by the Prosecution to meet its obligations in spite of the fact that they may have to work a little bit extra and maybe do things that they don't quite feel comfortable about doing, but nonetheless an order from the Trial Chamber is an order, and I think we all have an ethical and professional obligation to abide by the Court's order whether we like them or not. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for these comments. I'm going give the floor to the Defence. I just wanted to react to what you have just said. In the indictment, the criminal -- joint criminal enterprise, JCE, is described in 12 ways, numbered from page 9 to page 12. So there are 12 modes. I guess -- but I guess that mentally speaking it must also be the situation the Defence find themselves in. You are going to prove through your evidence each of these 12 modes. First mode: You say that the JCE was created, organised, funded, various government mechanisms. This is based on documents, I suppose. So at this present stage when you drafted this, you knew what documents, what testimony you were basing this on. What is there that prevents you or prevented you in the pre-trial brief to put in a footnote with references to it? Nothing prevented you from doing so. And there is nothing in here. In your filings, later on, you mention individual liability. Regarding Prlic, I see 24 cases under which, pursuant to 7(1) he could be accused of this or the other. There are 24 items, from page 12 in the indictment to 18. So I guess that out of the 24 cases, you are going to adduce evidence through witnesses or documents to say -- let's take (e). You say that he had the power to assign and to dismiss high officials. Well, I guess you're going to introduce documentary evidence showing that he had the power, the legal power, to assign or dismiss. I guess all this has been prepared already. So what is it that would prevent you from giving me a list of witnesses so that the Defence later, since they would know that you're going to introduce a given document through a given witness, they can prepare themselves for it. No. They can show that they did not have or he did not have the power to do that. So these are questions that are quite legitimate at this juncture. I'm going to go on, but I want everybody to express their views. You have the floor, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It seems to me that after the arguments presented by my learned friend Mr. Karnavas, there is practically nothing to add. However, I wish to point out that there is a logic involved here. If you have an indictment before you which is very exact and accurate in terms of specifying the charges brought against each and every accused person and evidence to support it, then practically all of this would not be necessary. However, what we have in front of us is a highly imprecise indictment. From the point of view of the Court, and especially from the point of view of the Defence, it is necessary to spell out precisely what evidence pertains to each and every one of the counts. It seems to me what you indicated in two cases, especially the latter example at the end of your remarks, all of that clearly indicates that the Prosecutor certainly had all this evidence concentrated when the indictment was being written, because truth to tell, there is no other way of writing an indictment. You have evidence, you have witnesses, and then you come up with the counts, the charges in the indictment. If that is the logic involved, it doesn't seem complicated to me to do all of that in the kind of table that you requested. I'm afraid that refusing to do that, or being unwilling to do that only works to the disadvantage of the Defence. That is why I fully support your proposal. I believe that it will make easier the work of the Court and considerably assist the work of the Defence in terms of fair proceedings in this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I fully subscribe to what my learned friend said. I just wish to say one more thing. It seems to me that from day one in our preliminary motions, we indicated that the indictment was very unclear, very imprecise, and that it was constructed as a kind of story into which six other persons could be fitted in, six other persons who held relatively high office in Herceg-Bosna, and it would only be necessary to change 17.1 and perhaps other paragraphs in the indictment describing every one of the accused. However, our attempts to get a clarification of the indictment through our objections totally failed, so it is with great relief and with great pleasure that we received your orders, Your Honour, that the indictment should finally be linked up properly to all the acts, all the accused, and to present proper evidence in terms of all the charges brought against the accused. That is why I would fully support your insistence that the Prosecution make this kind of table as soon as possible, and I think that this table is truly a prerequisite for all of us entering this courtroom trial-ready, that is to say the Prosecution and the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Valentin Coric fully subscribes to what our colleagues have already said, especially because we presented our objections to this effect in our pre-trial brief as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Pusic has no new comments to make and we don't want to engage in any kind of repetition in terms of what our colleagues have already said. I'm sure that the Prosecution is going to do what you asked them to do and within the deadlines requested. I just want to focus on what you've said in terms of the lengthy proceedings that you envisage. Perhaps this table would make it easier to expedite the matter. So maybe that is one of the ways in which the trial can be shortened. I shall make a small digression, since I already have some experience from the Hadzihasanovic-Kubura trial that I worked on. We worked four days a week, and that proved to be very useful, very beneficial in terms of consultations with our colleagues and everybody else involved. So I would like to subscribe to your proposal, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a second. Mr. Praljak wants to speak to us. Mr. Praljak, if you can hear us from Zagreb, where you are at the moment, what can you tell us? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to get up, or can I go on sitting? I do have something to say, Your Honour. When I heard that I would be accused before The Hague Tribunal, that was quite a while ago. This story has been bandied about for the past eight years, and I must say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Two sentences, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Praljak, hold on. I can hear you, but apparently the interpreters can't hear you. Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English channel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. We'll try again now. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can you hear me now and can the interpreters hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The English booth notes yes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May I start? All right. It's been eight years now that the Prosecution, at least in Croatia, has been saying that some people from Herceg-Bosna who held high office will be charged before The Hague Tribunal. At least 30 times I stated that in that case I will volunteer -- voluntarily surrender and seek to have the truth established before the Judges. Your Honour Judge Antonetti, during my initial appearance before you I said that the Prosecution is trying to speak from shards, thousands of shards from a mirror and trying to present the truth in that way. Let us hope that the Prosecution has good intentions as far as documentation is concerned, but I don't think they have good intentions. I think that the Prosecution knows how flimsy their evidence is, and they are trying to complicate the presentation of evidence as much as they can, although you've requested this. As far as I can remember, on the 30th of November, 2005, the Prosecution got an order from you, Your Honour, in terms of how they should deal with their evidence. An order is not something that the Prosecution can debate. They have to carry this out, just like I have to carry this out, just like I have to carry out every order that you've made. They did not do that, and they don't want to do that. And they are trying to place themselves on an equal footing with the Court. In my opinion, it is the Court that decides, and the Prosecution has to do the same thing that the Defence does. I think it is very regrettable that in The Hague often the Prosecution prevailed over the Trial Chambers. That is another -- there is another thing I wish to say. I have 250.000 pages in my computers. I have over 500.000 documents, 150 witness statements that I've already sent to The Hague to be translated. I sent over 25.000 documents, and my computer expert can act in accordance with your order and fill out your table exactly how you wanted it to be filled out. If I, with my meager financial resources, still on my own, can meet your request, then the only thing I can offer is that I give my own computer expert to the Prosecution so that they can get their documents organised as well. Your Honour, I came to The Hague immediately in order to have the truth established and in order to have a fair judgement passed. However, the intention of the Prosecution is different. It is true that crimes were committed. Quite a few of them, at that. However, in terms of the -- in terms of the actual liability involved and the responsibility involved and the bad history involved, there is nothing specified in the indictment. For example, in America there are 21 million crimes committed, 7 million of which are grave crimes, but on the basis of that you cannot come to the conclusion that there is a joint criminal enterprise involved. You have to call evidence on each and every one of the crimes. A war is a very difficult thing. I am going to ask for the trial to go on for a hundred years before they prove my liability, because I am fully convinced that what I did was only proper. Also, as far as my attorneys are concerned, I would like to thank you for the fact that this will hopefully be resolved as it should. My two attorneys, Mr. Kovacic and Ms. Pinter, were not there only for technical reasons, however I would like to ask them to come back, although they were away for a few months, but they are fully aware of the case and it would be very difficult for somebody else to be involved with the abundance of documents that has to be dealt with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Praljak. We've lost you. We can't see you on the screen any more, but we were able to hear you. It's 25 past ten. We will have a technical break now, and after the break I will give the floor to the Prosecution to allow them to respond to the Defence. It's 25 past ten. We will resume at five to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Before I give the floor to the Prosecution for them to answer, I want to point out the following: What I'm saying to the Prosecution now is something I'm going to tell to Defence counsel if they were not to comply with the instructions given by the Trial Chamber. I do not treat them differently. It is just so that in the pre-trial stage the Prosecution are on the front line because they are the first to adduce evidence. So that's the reason why I turn to you. But in the reverse case, I would have said the same to the Defence if they had not complied with their obligations. So I'm going to listen to you with great care. I would like you to answer what the Defence counsel and Mr. Praljak said, and the gist of it is that the Defence believe that you do not want to disclose this to keep an edge. You want to keep your advantage, which would be stupid at this stage. We're not here to keep an edge on the other party. The judicial process is an adversarial process which is done in all honesty between the parties, and if you do not want to disclose something in order to have an advantage over the other party, that would be totally stupid, all the more so since you know that in the end the Judges will assess the evidence individually, or every allegation will be checked, scrutinised very closely, so there is no advantage whatsoever. I believe it is in your interest to be as transparent as possible, and within this judicial arena to provide your evidence. You have started to do so in your pre-trial brief. You have to continue doing so through your witnesses and your evidence. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I want to start out by just clearing the air on the Prosecution's approach to this case, because a great deal of liberty has been taken with the nature and history of this case and the Prosecution conduct of this case in the last few minutes. A great deal of false information has been given to this Chamber, and there is a false story being given that I want to make clear is contrary to the fact. This Prosecution team has worked as hard or harder than any other Prosecution team that I am aware of to prepare this case, a large case, a complex case, to prepare it for trial in as efficient and effective way as possible. This Prosecution team knows its responsibilities. I have been prosecuting complex cases for the last 25 years in a common law system, and this is not the first large complex case that I've prosecuted. I do not have to be reminded by Defence counsel of my responsibilities. The Prosecution is anxious to present this case in as effective and efficient and fair way as possible, and we indeed have worked -- we tried to work with the previous Trial Chamber and with the Pre-Trial Judge and with the senior legal officer to move this case forward. We have done everything possible to move this case forward efficiently. We've tried -- we've proposed adjudicated facts. That motion was filed almost one year ago, on the 4th of April, 2005. We're trying to follow a very well-endorsed and accepted practice in the Tribunal of taking much of the evidence, especially the so-called crime base evidence, on paper. We have filed no fewer than four 92 bis motions dating back to the 30th of June last year for this to be done. All those motions are still pending. We have made extensive efforts to get agreed facts from the Defence. We made extensive submissions and exchanges with the Defence over a period of months on agreed facts, which led essentially, Your Honour, to nothing, to nothing from these six Defence teams. So we don't need to be reminded of that, but Your Honour might not be aware of that fact. Mr. Praljak said a few moments ago that he admits - and I quote from the transcript - he admits that "quite a few crimes were committed." I would like to know which crimes he admits were committed so we don't have to prove those. Mr. Praljak said he admits crimes were committed. Well, I'd like him to tell us which crimes in the indictment he admits were committed. This Prosecution team is doing everything possible to present this case. Its positions are not tactical or based on gaining advantage at all, and I fully reject out of hand Mr. Karnavas's attacks in particular as completely unfounded and completely unprofessional, and I will say right now that this Prosecution team will not stand by and let such accusations be made and not respond to them in full force. Extensive motions were filed, Your Honour, in this case, challenging the indictment. Many of the complaints you've heard this morning, Your Honour, go to the form of the indictment, the way the indictment is charged. Your Honour, there was extensive litigation on this before the previous Trial Chamber. Motions were filed and extensively litigated, discussed, and adjudicated. By and large the previous Trial Chamber rejected all of the Defence attacks on the indictment, with a few exceptions, and an amended indictment was prepared. But overall, the indictment as charged in this case was fully affirmed by the Trial Chamber and there is no point in the Defence getting up and going back and talking about those issues again. The Trial Chamber found the indictment fully sufficient, proper, legally sufficient and providing extensive information to these accused. And as I've said before, and I've looked at many indictments filed at this Tribunal in the last ten years, and this is one of the most detailed indictments that has ever been filed by the OTP to date. There was references to the JCE and the fact that perhaps other members of the JCE that are listed in the indictment, Kordic, Blaskic and others, they weren't charged with a JCE. Well, first of all, I don't think that's required at all. I don't think the fact that someone is named in a subsequent case as a member of the JCE, there's no requirement that that person be charged in their own indictment as a JCE, the Prosecution might proceed on an entirely different theory. So the fact whether Blaskic was charged under JCE or not is totally irrelevant for what's before this Chamber. I would say correct the record to say that in fact Mr. Kordic was charged. The doctrine at that time - as Your Honour well knows, the language and the nature of this doctrine has evolved through the years - back in those days this doctrine was being called the common purpose doctrine, and if one goes back and reviews the Kordic trial judgement and Kordic appeals judgement, you will find in fact that Mr. Kordic was, contrary to what was represented a few moments ago, charged and convicted based in part on a common purpose, or a JCE, theory. In terms of adjudicated facts, I've said before, Your Honour, I'll say it again: The Defence repeatedly dismisses these out of hand as if they're somehow completely irrelevant to this case. Your Honour, the proposed adjudicated facts come from closely related cases. Other Bosnian Croat cases, the Kordic case, the Blaskic case, the Tuta-Stela case, that are closely related to this case. These issues have not just been lightly treated; they have been actively fought, actively litigated, actively contested in these other cases, and at the end of the day, after extensive litigation, after extensive evidence on both sides by the Prosecution and the Defence, the Judges have made rulings. They've issued judgements, as you know, Your Honour, Judges do, and in those judgements they made findings of fact and they made conclusions on many points relevant to this case. This Tribunal has come under great criticism for how slow these proceedings are, that the same facts are litigated over and over and over again when they've been litigated in other cases, and Your Honour we have proposed extensive facts - did it almost a year ago - 515 facts from these other cases, and we're still waiting for a ruling on that. I've mentioned one specific example in particular, the existence of an international armed conflict. That issue has been litigated up, down, left, right, ten different times and every Judge - every Judge - in this institution, Trial Judge, Appeals Judge, every Judge who has looked at the issue has universally and unequivocally found the existence of an international armed conflict involving the Republic of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the extensive involvement and control of the Croatian government. Now, if we have to litigate those issues all over again when every Judge in this institution for the last eight years has found that already, we would suggest, Your Honour, that is a waste of judicial resources and should not be necessary. On the charts, Your Honour, I say again I want to make it very clear, I reject entirely any suggestion the Prosecution's not prepared to start its trial. We will. We will stand up on the 25th of April and we will make our opening statement, and following that we will call our first witnesses and we will -- we are prepared for this trial and we will go forward. The fact that certain charts in a certain way presenting certain information in a certain way using a particular format, the fact the particular charts have not been prepared to date is no reflection, has nothing to do with whether this case for the Prosecution is fairly and adequately prepared this case for trial. We have and we will and we'll go forward and we'll present this case, Your Honour, and, Your Honour, I think, will be ultimately be quite pleased with the way the Prosecution presents its case because it's going to be well organised and we'll present it to you as effectively as we possibly can. Now, I cannot speak for the Defence. I'm sure it's in the Defence interest to obstruct our case and delay our case and do everything possible to keep this evidence from coming in. I can't speak to them. All I can say is, Your Honour, that the Prosecution will do everything within its power to present this case to you and your colleagues in as effective a way as we possibly can. In terms of the charts in other cases Your Honour, based on the information I've been able to gather, including in the last 45 minutes, we stand, and I point this out by purposes of information -- let me preface my comments by saying, Your Honour, there is no resistance to doing the charts you've ordered, it's simply a matter of time and effort. And I again reject the Defence counsel who have stood up and said we think the Prosecution is being tactical, we detect some resistance on their part. That is false. That is completely wrong, and we reject it. We are prepared to do as much as we possibly can to prepare these charts, but they do come, Your Honour, with all great respect, late in the pre-trial process. This case has been in pre-trial for over a year with another Pre-Trial Chamber and another Pre-Trial Judge, and the Prosecution prepared its case under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and under the guidance and direction of another Trial Chamber and another Pre-Trial Judge. At no time in that history were these requirements set out or put upon us, so we prepared our case but not in the particular way, Your Honour, you would like us to prepare it. Now you give us the time and opportunity to do it, we will do it. We'll do everything in our power to provide the information that you desire. Now, let me make it very clear: We stand by our position, Your Honour, that no charts like this have in fact been provided or required in any other case except for, of course, Your Honour's other case, the Dragomir Milosevic case. I'll come to that case in a moment. But in no other case, and we checked, including the Stakic case, including the Blagojevic case, in no other such case was there anything similar to these kinds of charts required. Let me be very specific: In the Blagojevic case what was required was a list indicating the witness -- the name of the witness, a summary of the testimony, the paragraph of the indictment that the testimony related to. That's what was required in the Blagojevic case. That is exactly and no more than what Rule 65 ter on its face requires. It is no more and no different than what the Prosecution submitted to the Chamber on the 19th of January. What we submitted on the 19th of January, and I'm just -- I'm looking, for example, at page 38 of our witness list: The name of the witness, a summary of the witness's expected evidence, the counts of the indictment to which it relates, the paragraphs to which it relates, the relevant accused, and the expected time for the testimony. That is all or more than was required in the Blagojevic case, and there was nothing about linking exhibits or listing exhibits or linking exhibits to witnesses. This was for -- the first witness in the Blagojevic case started on the 15th of May, 2003, and a working copy of the very summary that I talked about that gives you all this information was first provided in that case on the 2nd -- on the 2nd of May, 13 days before the trial started, and it was a much limited -- much more limited than the information than Your Honour would like. The same as in the other cases. There was no such filing or requirement in the Stakic case. In the Blagojevic case, again, Judge Schomburg required a proofing chart, and that proofing chart was once again nothing more than what Rule 65 ter requires. The proofing chart gave the name of the witness, a summary of the witness's testimony, and the counts of the indictment to which they related. And we've done all of that. We've done absolutely all of that, and that's all that the proofing chart in the Blagojevic case required. And I have a transcript of that -- of a hearing before Judge Schomburg on that, where he talks about that. Judge Schomburg, the 27th of March, 2003: "To be quite clear on this, we shouldn't mix up apples and pears. This proofing chart is basically an outline based on the paragraphs of the indictment and telling us from the point of the view of the Prosecution what a witness allegedly will testify as to each paragraph and each count." That was all. And our 65 ter filing on the 19th of January do exactly that. In that case, in fact, that information was provided on a witness-by-witness basis approximately two days before each witness testified. That's when the proofing charts, the individual proofing charts, were required. There was one that was done pre-trial, about 14 days before the trial started, much more limited information, and then supplemental or additional proofing charts provided approximately two days before each witness testified. That's the story of the proofing charts in the Blagojevic case, Judge Schomburg's ruling. Your Honour, if we could go -- refer to some potentially confidential material and if we could go into private session for a moment, I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's move to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no resistance to doing this. The Prosecution is not being tactical. It's simply a matter of effort and time, and with the greatest of respect if -- if a new -- if a new referee comes into the game of football in the last period of the game and changes the rules of the game, and perhaps it's his prerogative to do so, and Your Honour if you want to ask us to do these charts, we will do everything we can to prepare them, but if it comes in in the last few minutes of the football game and each side has to then completely prepare its case in a different way, to change its game plan and organise themselves in a different way, it takes time. The only thing that the Prosecution has consistently said -- we said it before, we told to it your legal officers, we've said it in our filing on the 30th of January, I said it in the Status Conference on the 30th of January, the only thing we've ever said was if Your Honour indeed wants this information, we will do our very best to provide it to you but it cannot be done without a tremendous amount of time and effort. And we will do that. We are making our best efforts to do that now. We're working very hard, very intensively to prepare as much of this information for you as we can, and all I can ever promise, Your Honour, is to use my best faith -- good faith and best effort to do -- to satisfy Your Honour's wishes. That's all I can ever do, and we will do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott, for your explanations, and I do take note of your will and determination to do everything you can so that we can see the efforts you've made and to have the best situation to start the trial. In relation to what you have just said, you were referring back to previous cases, you are quite right; it is true to say at that before, we just had a witness list and a summary list of the contents of their testimony as well as some other information, but since then major things happened. Let me mention a few of them. First of all, the international community realised that if we kept up this pace, this Tribunal will work for another century. It was therefore decided in New York that a deadline would be set, and the deadline is 2010. On the basis of that time line, the OTP were asked to conclude their investigation. You were under the obligation to conclude your investigations and the so-called referral procedure was set in place under Rule 11 bis. But we did more than that. The Judges in this Tribunal, under the authority of President Meron, looked into the matter in order to see how to be most efficient in order to meet the caseload, cases prepared by the Prosecution. A committee was created. It was presided over by Judge Bonomy, and there were also other Judges, Judge Hanoteau, on that committee which gave a preliminary report, and last week we got its final report. This committee was officially announced in the Security Council in order to convey the message to the international community that this Tribunal and the Judges in particular were taking this thing very seriously and had established new procedures, among which we have the part played by the Pre-Trial Judge. This working committee concluded that the Pre-Trial Judge had to be fully committed to the pre-trial stage and had to settle upstream problems that, unfortunately so sometimes, crop up during the trial. So this is the spirit in which I committed myself, first of all. Not just this case, because initially I was not supposed on this case. I was supposed to be on the Pandurevic et al. case, Srebrenica 2 case, because I thought that I would be in charge of that case. But for reasons outside my control, some months ago I was told -- more exactly, the then-president told me that I would be sitting on the Prlic case. I didn't quite understand why there was this shift inasmuch as the Prlic accused were on provisional release, and I thought it was not that urgent to call this case, whilst the Pandurevic case was different. The accused were in detention, and I thought that it was better to start with that case, but for reasons I do not understand it was deemed necessary to decide otherwise. And this is how I came to be the Pre-Trial Judge. But from the very beginning, in keeping with the conclusions of the Bonomy report, I did not ask my senior legal officer to deal with the case, because that's usually how it used to be before. The senior legal officer would be the one who would call meetings between the parties and would try, at their level, to settle issues, and the pre-trial hearing presided over by the Pre-Trial Judge, as was done only yesterday, would take only 20 minutes and that would be it. This is not how I see the pre-trial stage. I believe all the problems have to be aired and solved so that the trial can be held in the best conditions possible. You stated that Rule 65 ter never mentioned the issue of charts or tables. You are absolutely right in saying so. But there's not just Rule 65 ter. There is Rule 90 and other Rules which make it necessary for the Trial Chamber to establish a witness list and an exhibit list. Now, how can you reasonably do so if you do not have something to go by? Moreover, you filed various motions for judicial notice of specific facts or for admission of evidence, statements coming from other cases, or under 92 bis. You know very well that Rule 92 bis makes it possible to admit written testimony under certain conditions, but, for instance, when it could be of cumulative nature. Now, how can I determine whether there is something cumulative under 92 bis as compared to another witness? I need to know the contents of the testimony of that other witness, and I have to check by reference to the other evidence. If I don't have that, how can I work? So there is the two ways of going about it; the classical way, which unfortunately was in force until now, where you prepare your list, as you just said, and you realise the magnitude of the problems during trial. The other option would be that the parties and the Pre-Trial Judge sit together to see under what conditions we can have a trial, fully complying with respective jurisdictions and skills and competencies. I don't think you are opposed to that. But today you are telling me that when the referee changes the rules of the game at the last minute, that raises problems for you. You're right. You're right. However, this is not the last minute. I've been talking about this for several months. And let's take up an analogy. Somewhere I'm the quarterback in American football. I'm trying to steer the game, everybody's game, so that the people looking at the game, but I mean at least that from the outside, one has the feeling that the pre-trial is efficient and quick. I do take note of the fact that you have only limited resources, that this is a Herculean task. I'm very well aware of it, because your job has been mine, or was mine several years ago. So I do know what it entails to be a Prosecutor. And since I know that personally, I'm in a position to tell you that if by the 24th of April you are not able to do all this work, just -- just try to have it done for the first wave of witnesses you're going to call. And if I understood properly, of course sometimes the Prosecution will change tack in midstream. I believe I understood that you first want to establish the political background, the historical background, to then move on to the JCE, and the Chamber will only hear evidence on crimes in municipalities toward the later stage, towards the end. So you still have enough leeway to get prepared and to let everybody know what you're going to do with your first witnesses and to let us know what exhibits you're going to produce through them. If I understood properly, we're going to have among the first witnesses expert witnesses. Well, they're going to come here, and they's going to testify so that the truth can be ascertained. The witnesses are going to speak to the then political background and situation, and you were seeking to have admission of 550 facts. If your request is not met, within a matter of seconds you can ask your expert witness whether he or she can confirm that on a specific date Mr. X or Y and Z met in order to prepare a decision by the government on a given point, and your expert witness will say, "Yes, indeed," because the Official Gazette mentions it. It takes a few seconds, no more, and it's done by your expert witness, and so on and so forth. This is one way to go about it. There again, this raises other problems. The expert witness, I guess that he's going to come up with the -- a report of 400, 500, maybe a thousand pages. You will seek to tender this report. We have six accused, and through their counsel they are going to make submissions. If you have a thousand pages from your expert, it is likely that each accused will have 50 or 100 pages of comments. If you multiply all those by six, you can imagine what a mountain of work we can expect on the Bench, because we have to make a decision on this report. So I have a worry there. You have expert witnesses. I don't know who is going to come so far, what they're going to speak about, what exhibits. We have to get prepared. You can't just say that in the last minute Mr. XYZ is going to come to speak about the Banovina area. So I think it's in your interest to prepare accordingly. Of course, the Defence will have to do their job. And I repeat it: We are here to make sure that the rights of the accused are preserved. This is about equality of arms. We are not in a system where you have an all-powerful Prosecution and then, snowed under by so much evidence, the Defence counsel could not fulfil their mission. The Judges are here to maintain or redress that balance without any bias, because we do not have any bias with regard to the allegations. It is only when we will -- or when we decide on the basis of the evidence, that we can decide, but now we don't know where we're going. But steer us in a given direction, this is what you do in your Prosecution case, and then we'll have the Defence. You have to present your case on the basis of evidence so that we, in all serenity, we can start the trial. So this is what I can offer you. I suppose you have a schedule. And I mentioned this to my colleagues in Trial Chamber II, and they told me that I have to ask you your timetable for the first months. If you have a timetable, you have the names for your witnesses, and also you know how many exhibits you're going to introduce. Of course when I told my colleagues that we were going to have 400 witnesses, they were amazed. I'm not so amazed because of the many facts in the indictment. And you are very right, and I want to congratulate, commend you on this. Your indictment is the most detailed indictment in the history of this Tribunal. It's true. Over a hundred pages, it is a very comprehensive indictment, which is good. Personally speaking, if I had been in your shoes, the indictment would have been a thousand pages long, given the scope. At least 1.000 pages.
