Well, everybody does their best, but in a case like this, in my view, everything had to be said so that pursuant to the principle of equality of arms people can meet the allegations, because if you have something general, how can you counter that? So I think we'll get there. We'll be able to start the trial on the 25th of April in the best conditions possible. I take due note of your intention, but I never doubted your intention. I do hear that you do not want to gain advantage over the Defence. Anyway, that would not have been appropriate, because to take up your analogy, remember that Judges are also referees, so if there is a mistake it will be sanctioned. So before we go any further, let me give the floor to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In the Blagojevic case, as in the Stakic case, the proofing chart was prepared. Whether it was prepared in the greatest of detail required by this Court, nonetheless one was prepared and an order was issued and an order was followed. In my tradition, which is the same tradition Mr. Scott comes from, when an order isn't complied by, especially if you were in a federal court, you would be sanctioned, and you would be sanctioned severely as an individual, and not be spared because you are a member of an organisation called the Office of the Prosecution. Mr. Scott says that over 25 years he has been working on complex cases, and I'm sure that he has. In preparing an indictment, one would think that, as he prepares it, he would have the name, what the person is going to talk about, how it relates to a particular element in the indictment, and any documents that would go to that. That in and of itself would be sort of the case map and the guide for preparing the chart. One would think as that as the case was prepared for -- additionally prepared for the investigative phase, every time you came across a document that was relevant to a particular element within a charge mentioned in the indictment, one would merely just put it into that folder. So I see no complexity in this procedure. As I noted earlier, one has to know their destination before they get there, and I would assume that before they filed this indictment - because after all the Prosecution files it when they're good and ready - one would think that they were absolutely ready. I dare say that the Prosecution has been preparing their case and continues to prepare their case by investigating continuously ever since they filed the indictment. And I go back and I say that had the Prosecution been prepared -- they should have been prepared at the moment the indictment was filed. However, we know from our own experience and from being in the field that witnesses continue to be -- major witnesses continue to be investigated, continue to be questioned, and they're still out there, trying to locate evidence to somehow support this highly comprehensive and detailed indictment. If you look at, Mr. President, 17.1, paragraph 17.1 of the indictment, and then you see -- you look at it, say how on earth can someone defend against all these different alternatives? Do they have a theory? If they have a theory for each and every one of them, every single word that is in that, they should be able to prove it. They should have it already. It shouldn't be a guessing game. And I do stand by my comments and I say so with all due respect to my friends on the Prosecution side, that to some degree, at least from our perspective, it appears as if this is a trial by ambush. Why do I say that? Because if they were prepared as they say they are prepared - they claim they will be on April 25th, but I dare say they should be prepared already, if not sooner - why is it so difficult for them to say here is the order of our witnesses so you can prepare in advance, Defence, because we don't want to have an unfair advantage -- because I'm going to get back to that obstructing and delaying comment that Mr. Scott made, which I find offensive -- but here is the list, here are the documents that we intend to use for each one of those witness. And in fact, if you read -- and here are the specific paragraphs to which this witness and these documents will go to. What's so difficult about that? Nothing. However, perhaps because we are in this mixed system and some are stuck in their own legal traditions, in the adversarial process, that is, that we fear that giving anything away to the Defence might be to our disadvantage because, after all, a weak Defence will ensure a conviction but not necessarily the truth. And so I say they should be prepared today - if not today, tomorrow - to give us a comprehensive list of all of their witnesses, the order in which they want to present them, in groups, in blocks, whether it's the political, the historical, the leadership, whatever that may be, so we can begin to prepare today. You talk about a Herculean task. Imagine being on this side, where we don't have that fleet of resources that is available to the Prosecution, where we're constantly having to struggle for finances. I'm going to be talking about that at some point, hopefully later on today. However, it makes it much more difficult for us to try to figure out what it is that they're trying to do. They talk about 92 bis motions. If they had a clear objective in mind from the beginning, and I dare say a good prosecutor, an organised prosecutor, one who is really wanting to be there for the truth and assist the Court, and of course his brethren on the other side, would have been able to say here are the list of all the 92 bis witnesses that we wish to present. You know, the written statements through 92 bis. What happens? As you recently noted, we just got another motion. That motion comes with a CD. That CD contains hundreds of pages of documents. So here, while I'm trying to prepare for the beginning of the trial, I'm having to deal with these sorts of matters. Now, it's not by accident. And why do I say that? Because I've been around the block too. I've been practising close to 25 years. I know how it works, and these are tactics that are used in order to bog down the Defence with these sorts of things rather than being prepared for trial. I don't blame them. The Rules don't say, look, you have to file it all in advance, but cry me a river when you talk to me about having worked so hard and trying to prepare this case, and in spite of all of that, they're unable to meet the Court's order of November 30th 2005. It doesn't make any sense. They talk about agreed facts. If you look closely at the agreed facts, Mr. President, you will see they're taken from the indictment. So what do they want me to do? They want me to agree to the indictment, slowly, incrementally, piece by piece out of context, taking agreed facts that are selected by them that suits their purposes, and they want me to do their job. They're here to prove their case beyond a reasonable doubt. The burden is on them, not on me. They need to do it, and I'm not here to help them. They talk about adjudicated facts. I couldn't agree more, to some extent, with Mr. Scott that these facts come from previous judgements. However, we must keep in mind a couple of things. One, as I noted earlier, if the indictment is structured in a particular way and it charges certain incidents, the lawyers in those cases may not necessarily challenge facts which the Prosecution obviously from the get go, from the -- and when I see this, it seems to me very clear that they already had this trial in mind when they began, sort of as a pyramid structure, this is how it's done in these complex cases. Because what do they do? They didn't charge everything, they didn't charge them with joint criminal enterprise, although they included certain things, and then they began to prove certain things, such as the international armed conflict, such as whether -- what was the structure of the HVO. Why? Because the Defence in those cases, with the limited resources and for tactical reasons, may not necessarily challenge that because it doesn't go to the nature of the crimes for which the accused is being charged. So if you're dealing with Blaskic, for instance, what were the big issues in Blaskic? It was basically the Lasva Valley incident and his role as a commander and whether he would have been responsible for any crimes that were committed. What does it have to do with the HVO leadership what the Herceg-Bosna was -- the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was trying to accomplish, whether it was a state within a state? All these issues that of course are relevant in this particular case. So if I'm the accused in that particular case, and I have limited resources, as we all do, I might try to focus on the very strict nature of the crimes for which I'm being -- I'm committed. And that's why we find offensive to try to certain -- to just accept adjudicated facts when we know now, having the benefit of more documents, more archives, more resources, that perhaps some of those adjudicated facts were wrongly founded, and it's our obligation to challenge. And of course the Prosecution has stated its position. I in good faith apply the technique that was used in the Blagojevic case, which was we can take an adjudicated fact, if we can agree on some common language, to tweak it so that it's more -- that it's put into context, that adjudicated fact then becomes an agreed fact and thereby it's a stipulation. The Prosecution over and over, and you can go back and look at the transcripts, Mr. Scott was like a broken record. Over and over again he objected to this concept, as if somehow I was doing violence to these adjudicated facts when in fact all I was merely suggesting is if we put them in context and if we can agree to some common language that would be both beneficial to the Prosecution and to the Defence, then these would be stipulated facts not subject to dispute, you know, and it won't be just a mere presumption. It would be a fact upon which you, Your Honour, and your colleagues could -- could rely on in reaching your -- making your findings of facts and conclusions of law. So in -- very briefly, I just want to say that I still believe that the Prosecution, while they're trying their level best, can do better. And I'm hopeful that we can work with the Prosecution. I'm not predisposed to trying to work out in advance a manner and means by which we can all go forward. I do take exception to Mr. Scott saying, well, you know, as Prosecutors they're professional and somehow the sleazy Defence lawyers on this side, they obstruct, they delay, we know what they're all about, you really can't trust them. When we come into this court, Mr. President, I'm as equal as the Prosecution. He is no more higher than I am. I sit at the same level. He has no more power than I do. And his voice is no more important than mine, he is no more credible than I am. We all stand by our word. We all know that. And I take exception to the Defence being characterised as a bunch of hoodlums trying to obstruct and delay the process. We're here as professionals. We have a job to do. We are in a position where we have to challenge the credibility of the witness, the credibility of the documents; that's our job. And if we do our job properly and if by any chance a conviction is then found, at least we can all rest assured that the evidence was tested properly and the accused got a good defence, and the Judge, based on the evidence that he heard in this rather adversarial proceeding, arrived at the right conclusion. So I do take exception to being characterised as someone who obstructs and delays. With those comments, Your Honour, I have nothing further to add with respect to what has been just discussed, only to suggest that the Prosecution should be ordered - if not ordered, cajoled, perhaps - to provide us as soon as possible with at least the first group or groups of witnesses that they intend to introduce and all of the exhibits, all -- everything that they intend to rely on. It makes it easier for us if I know that the first ten witnesses will be experts, I know their names, I know what they're going to be relying on. I can begin to prepare in that fashion. Short of that, I'm constantly trying to figure out what is next, and to get it one week before trial is not good enough. They're not obligated to do that. It may be because Mr. Scott comes from a federal system, perhaps, where in a federal system in the United States you're not entitled to any evidence other than your client's statement until you get to court. So there we have sort of this dancing in the dark, as it were, for the Defence. Maybe that's the habit he's bringing over here, I don't know, and I don't think so, but I think that he could help us and he could assist the Trial Chamber, because also, as you well know, you and your colleagues must be prepared for the questioning, and the sooner you have that information, the sooner that you can begin in looking at that information. And again I have no reason to believe that they're not acting on good faith, but I do think that we all come with our own traditions and our own habits, and perhaps sometimes our habits get the best of us. But I don't want to suggest in any way, shape, or form that I believe that they're not acting in good interests, however, I think perhaps they may be playing a rather clever game, all within the bounds of the Rules, but nonetheless it does put us at a grave disadvantage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The other lawyer?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be brief and I'll say this: I have to notice that I did not wholly understand the presentation made by my learned friend Mr. Scott because in what he said we noted a contradiction. My colleague says that the Prosecution is ready to go ahead with the trial on the 24th or, rather, the 25th April, and on the other hand there is quite obviously resistance in complying with the request made by the Court, which is very important for the Defence. It seems to me to be quite logical that if the Prosecution stands trial-ready on the 25th and -- 24th or 25th of April, that in fact they have all the material the Court requires of them. Therefore, I consider it logical just for them to hand it over to the Court in the manner and way in which the Court has asked for it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have nothing to add to what my colleagues have already said, so I fully endorse all the positions and proposals made by Mr. Karnavas and my colleague Ms. Senka Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Defence for Valentin Coric also would like to join in with what my colleagues have already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I also come from a system where we respect Court orders, as Mr. Karnavas has already said, but I did not gain the impression that Mr. Scott wishes to say he does not wish to comply with the Court order. What I understood him to say was that he would comply, as is fit that he does. All I would like to say is this; that partial compliance in a month or two would not be that bad for contributing to what we asked. It would be, of course, much better for us if we had the list straight away, a comprehensive list with all the documents on it, as you have indeed requested. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] By ruling of the Court on the 13th of November, 2005, it expressly states that Mr. Scott has to compile the charts. In response to Mr. Scott, the provisions of the Court and the Court order and ruling which goes under the heading of "Headlines --" of "Guidelines," but that Mr. Scott treats the Court as a party with which he can deliberate without any appeals and the provision takes the form of guidelines. From the 30th of November to the present day, had there not been any resistance, a chart could have been compiled as was instructed by the Court. And from this we are able to conclude that the question is not a technical one but one of substance, and it is one of substance because putting all the documents in order, compiling charts for witnesses and so on and so forth will topple the indictment of Mr. Scott, and therefore he would like, as we would say colloquially, he would like to have murky waters to fish in. Now, as far as that famous problem that we've talked about, what can be taken from previous trials and previous proceedings, is this: Many assertions were made about the facts, whereas too little facts were quoted, and I'm going to quote just a few facts, not to take up too much of your time. Nowhere is it stated that 12.000 wounded persons were treated, that is wounded Muslims were treated in Croatian hospitals. When I say 12.000, then Mr. Scott would have to know that there were 720.000, the same as America treating 700.000-odd or 100.000-odd, if you're talking about France. It would cost 72 million -- billion dollars for America to do that and it would cost France 30 billion, and that all this was going on in a country that was occupied to one-third of its territory, that it had 15.000 dead and wounded, or 30 -- 40.000 wounded as well, and this was never stated. It was never stated that Croatia took over 340.000 refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, that it paid for them, that humanitarian aid arrived only in the form of food. Nowhere is it stated that one brigade from Rijeka, for example, was made up a thousand men that went to fight in the BH army, and therefore it was Croatia's involvement into the war but in the army of BH in this case, and the 500 and 600 names were never listed, that on the territory of the Republic of Croatia continuously Bosniak Muslims worked to arm the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was never mentioned. Nor did we have tables and charts saying how many thousands of tonnes of ammunition went over there. This Court never discussed the 227 documents of Franjo Tudjman which relate to Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it was just the rumours going round the corridors that were discussed. And that is why these proceedings, Your Honour, is important for historical truth, to determine the role played by Croatia, what certain indictees did over there, and that is why this trial -- it is important that this trial take on all the forms and shapes which would lead to the truth without fishing in murky waters, as Mr. Scott was prone to do until now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll now move on to another point, but let me say that next week I will issue an order clarifying all these issues, requesting a very specific schedule as of the 25th of April for the months of April, May, and June, with the list of witnesses and exhibits to be used. Let me now move on to another point, something I mentioned earlier on, but I did not get any straightforward answer about this. It is a matter that is of great interest to the Defence. Regarding the admissibility of evidence, of exhibits. A solution would be to avoid discussions beforehand about the exhibits, including American-style, American-type objections about such-and-such document as not being relevant, as not having any probative value, et cetera, et cetera. In many Trial Chambers, this issue has been solved in a very efficient way, and if we look at the Milosevic case, we can see that there are very few objections raised when it comes to the admission of exhibits. So now I'd like to turn to the Defence to get very quickly their position on that specific issue. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. When I listened to your earlier remarks regarding the admissibility of evidence, I could not put it more eloquently and succinctly. I totally agree with you about the way the Rules have been fashioned in this Court, and I totally agree that barring one exception, and that would be authenticity, normally the procedure has been and perhaps should remain that evidence should come in provided there is some indicia of reliability as well, but I don't think that that's going to be much of a problem. The way I have practised before, and the way I will continue to practice, is if I see a document that the Prosecution wishes to put forward, especially if I know in advance what documents they intend to put forward on a particular day and I have some advance notice, if I have any objections, I tend to raise them first with the Prosecution, alerting them to what I believe might be some problems in trying to reach some sort of agreement. If there is a problem with respect to authenticity, obviously I will be objecting, but normally I know that the documents come in, and I fully agree with -- with you, Mr. President, that simply because a document is admitted it doesn't mean that it will -- it will be given any particular weight. That is for you to decide based on the totality of the evidence and other matters as well. The cardinal rules that I tend to believe in are: Is a document authentic? Is it reliable in the sense that it hasn't been tampered with? And of course it's relevant, and even once it's relevant we still need to do the probative test. So I believe that you've articulated quite nicely. In fact, I noted to my colleague here that I wanted to take out that excerpt of the transcript because I think it's quite instructive. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I fully agree with what Mr. Karnavas has said and your proposal given today. I think that the possibility of subsequently challenging authenticity is something that will ensure a fair defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I also consider that your instructions this morning and your arguments that any complaints and objections should boil down to the question of authenticity and is in keeping with court practice and legal practice, and I think that that is what we should do in this trial, too, and leave the question of relevance for later on when evidence is produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as the Defence of Mr. Coric, I do agree in principle with what my colleagues said before me. However, I should like at this point in time to emphasise something that I noticed. The experience gained in these trials, these legal proceedings, lead me to observe that in the period before the indictment was raised that there was some manipulation with documents in different archives on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and unfortunately, part of the documentation from those archives is still lacking and inaccessible, and that perhaps or when we are thinking of admissibility of evidence, one should bear in mind the admissibility of the Presidency transcripts, that the Prosecution is basing a good part of its Prosecution case on. And we must also take into account the problems with intelligence data and documentation, that is to say documents that come from intelligence sources which very often came into being subsequently. Or if it was contemporaneous with the event, very often it was compiled with a lack of documentation of the event but are masking the real reasons behind an event. So I think that when a decision is made on admissibility of documents, we must bear in mind what I have just said, those considerations as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Apart from the comments made by Mr. Karnavas, which I fully endorse, as indeed I do what the other Defence counsel said, I don't wish to make any comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, we are dealing with a highly technical issue, but you might have your own opinion about it. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have nothing to add to what you yourself have said and what Mr. Karnavas has said, but the fact is that many major forces have tried to hide the truth about the war in our territory, or distort it to serve some other purposes and aims and not the truth, and in that respect we have many forgeries, falsifications which are quite evident, which intend to show something in a different light than it was, but that is your decision ultimately. So I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for that comment. Of course, when an exhibit is put forward and if the Defence says that they challenge the exhibit because they have information showing that the document is a forgery, of course the Chamber will take it into account, but of course the Defence will have to prove that the evidence, that the exhibit is a forgery. It's not enough that you say it is a forgery; you have to explain why it is so. In any case, I note -- I take note that we've made a lot of progress on that issue. I take note of that with a great deal of satisfaction. What I'm saying is valid for you too. When you put forward exhibits, the Prosecution will have also to apply the same conduct, not just merely saying objection, probative value, everything. But of course if the Defence put forward an exhibit that is a forgery, of course the Prosecution will be entitled to challenge it. Mr. Scott or Mr. Mundis, about that last issue, would you like to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I may. Just very briefly. First off, I just want to express my appreciation for Mr. Karnavas's comments and confirming that in fact the Office of the Prosecutor is acting in these matters in all good faith and doing the very best we can. I also, Your Honour, taking up the Court's last comments, I just want to put a line under what you just said. It's all too easy in the experience at this Tribunal for counsel to stand up and allege that a document has been forged or falsified in some way, but I completely agree with Your Honour that the mere allegation or the mere assertion by counsel is not sufficient. And if any counsel, either the Prosecution or the Defence side, make an allegation that a document is inauthentic or is forged or falsified, we will certainly expect that they immediately provide the basis for that and not mere -- not their mere assertion. Your Honour, we would like to -- we would like to address the question of documents as well because it's also very important to us, because indeed it is the Prosecution that will initially have the burden of presenting its evidence. The Defence, if it chooses -- if they choose to present evidence and if they choose to present their own case, that, we can all agree, is sometime in the future. So of course the presentation of evidence and the manner in which Your Honour wishes to proceed is of the great -- is of great importance to the Prosecution since we are the ones that will have to go forward first. In that respect, Your Honour, I have to say, to be perfectly transparent with Your Honour, a bit concerned about the admission of the exhibits, because we noted in your Status Conference on the 8th of November and again the 30th of January, that you had indicated, quite clearly, we thought, that you were inclined and intended to admit all the tendered numbered exhibits prior to trial. That would be the way to proceed. You said this on the 8th of November at pages 329 to 331 of the transcript, and you said that again on the 30th of January at pages 61 and 62 of the transcript, that you were inclined to number and admit all the exhibits prior to trial. Now, taking our guidance from what Your Honour said, we have prepared several motions that we have filed in the last 30 or 60 days, first concerning the so-called UN documents, and then concerning the ECMM documents, and then finally, and before there was a ruling -- I want the record to be clear: Before there was a ruling on the ECMM documents, we had also filed a similar motion on the so-called Spanish Battalion documents. Now, I have to tell Your Honour that we thought we were acting completely consistently with Your Honour's wishes to indeed accept and admit the exhibits prior to trial. So we were in fact a bit surprised and a little disappointed, if I might say, to receive the rulings on the 3rd of February and 9th of February indicating that none of this would be allowed and it would just kind of be the old-fashioned common law way, one document by one document. It's going to take a long time, with 9.500 documents, to admit them one at a time on a day-to-day-to-day-to-day witness-to-witness basis. We were also concerned that we're getting a bit mixed messages, Your Honour, with all respect to you and with all respect to the Chamber. On the one hand we were told in the Status Conference how you would like to proceed and we try to conduct ourselves accordingly, and yet then we get orders from the Chamber as a whole that seem to us to be completely contrary to the guidance that you have given to us. There are also indications, Your Honour, in some of the recent decisions - the one on the 3rd of February and the 9th of February - that many of the pre-trial issues in fact cannot be resolved and will not be resolved until the Ad Litem Judges are in place and the actual Trial Chamber that will hear this case is in place. I think Your Honour, based on your observations today, is astute enough to know the problems that presents for us. That means, if I understand these rulings correctly, that there are a large number of pre-trial matters which will not be resolved until after the Ad Litem Judges get here. And you've indicated several times, and I've confirmed it in speaking with other members of this institution, that the Ad Litem Judges will not arrive until approximately two weeks before this case starts. Now, Your Honour, that flies entirely in the face of pre-trial management. If the practice of this Tribunal is to be that pre-trial motions and issues can't be resolved except only two weeks prior to trial, that is not sufficient and that is not a good practice for anyone. It's not good for the Chamber, it's not good for the Prosecution, it's not good for the Defence. So we just simply point this out and would have to say that if that in fact is the intention of the Chamber and the intention of how to proceed, we have to alert the Chamber that we would fully expect that once the Ad Litem Judges arrive on approximately perhaps the 12th or the 10th to the 12th of April, we would be filing a number of motions then after they arrive that will need to be resolved, or renewing motions that have been filed in the past, like the ones that have just recently been denied. We will renew and file those motions again after the Chamber is fully constituted with the Ad Litem Judges and put those motions in front of the actual Trial Chamber. Let me give you a specific example, Your Honour. As you've indicated yourself today, this Tribunal has endorsed the practice of using 92 bis evidence. We have tried to do that. We've made several filings to that effect. Some of these witnesses who would be proposed 92 bis witnesses may indeed lay the foundations for certain documentary evidence which -- that -- concerning that evidence, we might choose to use some of that evidence early in our trial. However, until we know -- until the 92 bis motions are ruled upon and until we know whether that evidence has been admitted, makes it very difficult to plan how to proceed with particular exhibits and particular related evidence because we don't know if those statements have been -- will be admitted or not. The point of that, Your Honour, is to say that we would very much appreciate the Chamber's additional, very detailed guidance on how it wishes to proceed with the admission evidence. We had thought -- we had thought that we had heard the Chamber say that it wished to admit this evidence prior to trial, but now there are some indications that seem quite the contrary. So the Prosecution, Your Honour, would very much appreciate particular guidance on the admission of exhibits. We have numbered all the exhibits. They're all pre-numbered. They're all on our exhibit list, and if we can offer them all at one time ... We thought we would offer them in certain relevant batches; the UN documents, the ECMM documents, the Spanish Battalion documents. There might be other bundles or batches of documents in the future that are all logically related to each other from a particular collection. We had thought that was a reasonable way to proceed, but we would very much invite Your Honour's additional guidance on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're quite right in your comments, and I will indeed provide you with a number of clarifications. First of all, we are faced with the difficulty that you're aware of. The current Trial Chamber - myself, Judge Parker, Judge Agius - is not the Chamber that will hear the case. The Chamber that will hear the case will be made up by myself and two Ad Litem Judges. You have to keep this in mind. Secondly, second important item I would like to mention, when I requested that you prepare charts with the exhibits, and you did it with exhibits listed chronologically, I asked you to give them numbers. You complied. So you've accomplished 70 per cent of the work I requested from you. The 30 per cent to be done is to establish the link between the exhibits and the witnesses. I also told you, and maybe there was a lack of clarity on my part in that respect, I also stated that according to me, the de jure admission of exhibits happens when the witness is in court and when the exhibits are put to the witness. Why is it so? Because then there will be a debate with the Defence, because otherwise if we do not proceed that way, if we enter -- admit a document, let's take the example of the Spanish Battalion documents, if we admit the documents, we are talking about several dozens of documents, the Spanish Battalion documents are admitted. Let's suppose that you do not call any witnesses from the Spanish Battalion. What happens then is that the Defence will not be in a position to cross-examine people from the Spanish Battalion. Therefore, you will be placed at an advantage, unduly so, because the exhibits have been admitted there might not be a discussion about these exhibits. Personally speaking - and the two other Judges share my position, I must say - personally I would like to invite you, I would like to encourage you to do the following: These motions, 92 bis motions or other motions should be filed with the Trial Chamber that will hear the case, not with the current Trial Chamber, because the current Trial Chamber is not the one that is going to hear the case. I believe that it is up for the triers of fact to say the law and to assess the exhibits. It's not up to the Judges who are not going to hear the case to rule in any way about these exhibits. As a result, the charts you've provided have been numbered. We are going to stay with these numbers. These numbers have been given for identification purposes. For example, as for the Spanish Battalion documents, we only need one witness from the Spanish Battalion for all the exhibits to be admitted once the witness comes to testify. As for the admission of exhibits, it is made through an oral or written decision that occurs during the trial and not before the trial, because, as I said before, once a document has been admitted, if no one mentions the exhibit again, at -- when it comes to issuing the judgement, the Judges will be able to use that exhibit but the Defence will not have been able to raise the issue of that particular exhibit. And as I said before, once a witness is here in the courtroom, when you put a document to him, let's say -- let's take the example of the Spanish Battalion documents. You put to the commander of the Spanish Battalion one or two documents. You refer to a specific paragraph, and the Defence might cross-examine about this specific paragraph as well or other passages in the document. It's quite possible that the Judges will ask questions about other passages of the document, but there might be paragraphs of the document that have not been raised when the witness is here, but it's quite possible that the Judges later on realise how important the other passages of the document are, and they might very well rely on the rest of the document. That's why I very quietly, very clearly said last time, I very clearly warned everyone here that when we have a document, we are talking about the entire document, the document in its entirety. I noticed that we have a document amounting to 395 pages. It's a report from the Prosecution. Three hundred and ninety-four, 95 pages. There might be only one question about the document. I would be very surprised if questions were raised about every single page of this 394-page document, but I as a Judge will receive the 394 pages, and I will read them, all these pages, and I might very well refer to one paragraph of these -- of this document that has not been cross-examined or raised during the examination-in-chief because the document had been admitted beforehand. So in order to be extremely clear on that point, I would like to state that the chart you have prepared, that you have partly included in your pre-trial brief and that you might use later on, it's a chart that is there. It's very useful because we have dates in this chart, numbers in this chart, but you will need, when witnesses -- witnesses come to testify, you will need to put the documents to the witnesses. As for 92 bis, we are considering the matter with the other Judges. Personally, I would be in favour of referring the matter to the Trial Chamber that will hear the case. So for the time being, you should say the following, you should think the following: We have 400 witnesses. We have to prepare the examination of these 400 witnesses. We know, of course, that some of these witnesses will not show up. Some will die in the meantime. Some will disappear. We won't have 400 witnesses in the end, but you have to work on the assumption that 400 witnesses will come here to testify. And later on, you might possibly realise that you've called a witness and that another witness who was on the list is not necessary any more because the first witness already -- has already said anything. But in any way, in your plannings -- in the planning phase you have to work with the list of 400 witnesses. Only during the trial will you realise that some witnesses are not useful any more and they do not need to be called and part of their testimony could be admitted under Rule 92 bis, subject, naturally, to the right of the Defence to have these witnesses here in the courtroom to cross-examine them, although in some cases the Defence my decide not to cross-examine the witnesses. I hope I have clarified the issue. You should work on the assumption that the 400 witnesses will come here to testify. But then later on, once we have the two Ad Litem Judges, we'll have to deal with these issues. The two Ad Litem Judges will start from scratch, and once they see the cubic metres of documents, they will go -- undergo an emotional shock and they will need some time to recover. Of course we are dealing with professional Judges and they will get down to it very quickly. So you have to work on the hypothesis that your motions are not moot. The fact that they've been denied does not really -- does not matter. You can reintroduce your motions once the trial has begun. I hope I have been clear enough about the issue of documents. Now, once -- when comes the time for the Defence to cross-examine, I suppose you will use documents during the cross-examination. So in order for you to start working already, what I would like you to do is, when the Prosecution witness is here and you all have your documents, I don't know if they will be exactly the same documents, it's up to the various Defence teams to agree with that, but what I would like you to do is to submit your documents to the Judges. If you have 15 documents or 15 binders of documents, you will -- you will want to -- or 15 documents you want to use during the cross-examination, I would like you to give these documents to us for me and my colleagues to be able to read these documents, because with the e-court system, I can't move from one document to the next. So I will need the hard copies of the documents you want -- you will be using during cross-examination. I know that some of you are very familiar with that system, that practice I've just outlined, so I don't think it should be -- it should pose any difficulty to any of you. If there is no other issue with regard to the documents, I would like to raise another issue before we break. This will probably go down in history as the longest Pre-Trial Conference ever, but let me move on to the last item on the agenda before we start. Practice has shown that during the pre-trial stage, and also during trial, the Prosecution continue with their investigations. They do so in order to obtain new documents, in order to produce new witnesses that they had not scheduled. Mr. Karnavas mentioned this earlier on. As you know, it may well be that at the end of the Prosecution case, and after the Defence have started their Defence case, call their first witnesses, it may well be that the Prosecution came up with a request for reopening the case. Our case law is very clear about this, and I just want to spell it out for you. In so doing, you do not want to be prejudicial to the accused. I believe that if a -- there is an undergoing investigation, the Chamber must be alerted to it, and the Defence must be told that the Prosecution investigation goes on, without giving any details concerning a given individual. However, when you receive a document, so says the case law, you are under the obligation to disclose it straight away to the Defence. You should not keep it for weeks if not months. Indeed, let's imagine you receive the document in June without disclosing it to the other parties, and if six months later you want your case to be reopened, you know what the result will be: It will be denied. So this is what I advise you to do: Do read what the Kubura -- Hadzihasanovic-Kubura Chamber issued as a ruling, because it says it all. So this is what I wanted to tell you so that you are all in the know of things and the Defence counsel know it. They know that the Prosecution investigation goes on, but you get documents when you investigate, and under Rule 66 and 68, such documents must be disclosed. If there is a motion for reopening because of late disclosure, you can rest assured it is not likely to be granted. We're going to break for about 20 minutes. We'll start at ten past one [as interpreted], and we'll stop at quarter to two, because that's what the trade union rules say. We won't be able to deal with all the items, but anyway, we'll meet again soon.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, ten to one. Interpreter's correction: We'll resume at ten to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. We have an hour to look into the other matters on the agenda. First of all, I'd like to deal with the duration of the cross-examination. We mentioned this last time, and I seem to understand that there had been contacts between the Prosecution and the Defence. The new counsel who is going to be appointed - I hope it will be Mr. Kovacic - of course, he will join you in the Defence's meetings with the Prosecution so as to best prepare cross-examination. I'm going to give you the floor to take stock of the situation, but some preliminary observations before I do so. On the basis of the witness list and the scheduled length of the examination-in-chief, you have some indicia. Of course you need the documentary evidence, but you will get that very shortly, so you have an idea of the likely duration of the direct examination. As was stated by the Prosecutor, he initially intends to call witnesses as to the general political, military, or geographical background. So inevitably, we will be steeped in the very heart of the matter as presented by the Prosecution when it comes to the topic of the joint criminal enterprise. I don't know what everybody's position is, but I have an idea, and I imagine that there may be differences appearing among the accused or a different way of looking at a given problem. Then the accused, through their counsel, will be in a position to cross-examine the Prosecution witnesses as they wish. So two options are open: It may well be that the Defence teams will agree among themselves, notwithstanding their differences, so that there will be only one main counsel, as it were, who will lead the cross-examination, whilst the other Defence counsel may intervene on side issues. If there is a failure by the Defence counsel to agree, then we will have to have a fair breakdown of time allotted for cross-examination. So these are very complicated matters, as you see. You might say that the Judge is there to make a decision. Of course that's his job if there is a problem. But as you know, the Judges would rather see the problem solved upstream, because when it is done so, it's much better for everybody, because if a Judge makes a decision, of course, there's always one person happy with the decision, another unhappy. Sometimes two people involved are unhappy with the decision. So that the Judges don't have to decide, you must agree. I don't know whether you can agree or to what extent you can agree amongst yourselves, but I told you last time, for the sake of fair trial and the equality of arms, it is my initial feeling, but of course I will talk about it with my fellow Judges, but my impression is that if an accused, to be defended properly, if the direct examination took three hours and he needs three hours, well, he used the three hours. I find it difficult to say to an accused you only have an hour whilst the Prosecution would have had three hours. Of course, ideally speaking, if the Prosecution need three hours, there should be an agreement among Defence counsel. But failing such an agreement, we'll have to see case by case. In the beginning, we might have the most problems with the first witnesses, especially if they speak about political matters. But there may be, as it were, hard cores within the political matters which may be agreed on by the various accused, but it'll be up to you to tell me so. Mr. Scott, how far have you got -- well, Mr. Mundis, how far have you got in your discussions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Following the last Status Conference where this issue was addressed, last week we submitted a letter to the Defence, asking them if they had come up with a common proposal or counter-proposal that could be a starting point for moving discussions forward. I understand, perhaps in light of commitments attendant to the pre-trial briefs being filed by the Defence, that perhaps this was not an issue that they were able to spend much time on, but the way we left it after the last meeting was the Defence would discuss it amongst themselves and get back to us with some kind of proposal or counter-proposal to the one we had advanced at our initial meeting. We sent a letter last week and to date I haven't heard anything back from the Defence, so I don't really at this point have anything further to report on this matter from the Prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have the floor. Mr. Karnavas, you were lucky, in a way, because you were in a case with four accused, in the Blagojevic case, so you are experienced in the matter. I only know the case I sat on where we had two accused, but I think with four is better than with two, isn't it, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, at some point they did -- a couple of them pled out, Your Honour. But I have been in multiple cases, and here is my approach, Your Honour: Each witness has to be dealt separately. Once I see who the witness is, irrespective of the amount of time that the Prosecution intends to take with that witness, depending on what that witness has to testify to, I can pretty much guesstimate the amount of time that I would need to cross-examine that particular witness. Having said that, much of what I might cross-examine on might be about 90 per cent of what all of us would want to cross-examine on anyway because of the nature of the witness. Of course, I would intend to rely on contacts with my colleagues, but at the end of the day, I want to make it rather clear that my obligation is one to my client and to make a very clear record in the event this case finds itself before the Appeals Chamber, and that is my primary concern, is making a very, very clear record, both so at the end of the trial I can point to the record concretely for the trial bench as to what they should look at in trying to find alternative plausible explanations to the circumstantial evidence upon which the Prosecution is going to rely on in making its arguments. So I need to make my record. I would be able to -- in advance, to guesstimate how long it would take, and I believe that would be useful for the Trial Chamber. I have spoken with some of the members of the Defence team and sort of -- I don't want to use the word "lobby," but I have spoken with them. When Mr. Kovacic was still on the case I have had extensive dealings with him. He's an extremely professional lawyer with experience, and he is of the like opinion that you should only cross-examine on what is absolutely relevant and of assistance to the Trial Chamber, and I think that's what I intend to do. I'm sure my colleagues will probably feel the same way. Our approach will be, probably, that we will be consulting each other to talk, to find out in advance and what points each of us wish to make, and perhaps the first person who would be cross-examining would be making many of the points with the others perhaps adding to it, depending on the witness. It would be my position, and I would stick to it unless ordered to do otherwise, that since Mr. Prlic is at the top of the list, that we go first on every single witness. I say this not because I view him as the most important individual, although as my client he is, but he is the first person on the list and he is at the apex of the indictment given that the others who are in this joint criminal enterprise will be tried in absentia. And I say this with all due respect, but I'm sure the Prosecution intends to be prosecuting the late President Tudjman, the late Susak and Mate Boban and the others. So we are going to be going first. However, there may be instances where I will not need to cross-examine at all and I may reserve my -- my cross-examination to maybe asking a question or two at the end, it all depends. I certainly will try to abide by any timetables the Trial Chamber imposes on me. However, I can certainly say that in the previous case that I had before Judge Liu, who runs a rather tight but fair ship, we were always able to meet the time constraints because I believe as long as I could demonstrate in good faith that I was cross-examining in an area that was fertile for the Defence, establish that it was relevant to a particular defence, Judge Liu was kind enough and generous enough to allow me to pursue that, and of course I did not abuse that, and I think that's one of the things that you will have -- you and your colleagues will have to judge us by; that is, we will need to establish our bona fides each and every time we stand up with the Trial Chamber. I might add, just as an example, the Prosecution in that particular case brought in a Mr. Butler, one of these homegrown, in-house what they call experts. Actually, he was an OTP employee who had since left. And I say that because that's what he was, an employee who they characterised as an analyst who then testified as an expert. He testified on direct examination for five days. My cross-examination alone was six days of Mr. Butler, and I believe counsel for Mr. Jokic had one full day and then there was a day for re-direct and re-cross-examination, and I believe at the end of the 11 or 12 days that the Trial Chamber had very few questions. That's an exception, although there were others that were four days or two days or three days, but that's just to give you an example. One of the things that I also wish to point out, that there may be instances where the Prosecution will be trying to tender a witness that will bring in their expert report, for instance, and they may only question the witness for half hour, an hour, and then more or less resting on the report itself. And of course under those circumstances, we should be entitled to full and fair cross-examination. That was done in previous cases. I know in one particular case there was a demographer, Mr. Broomberg. He came in, it was no less than an hour on direct, and he was on the stand for two hours being cross-examined -- two days. He was -- for two full days he was cross-examined, all of which was relevant. Another example was Mr. Deronjic. I believe he testified for one day, I cross-examined him for four days. Again, all of it was relevant and pertinent to the case and Judge Liu allowed me to do so based on my professionalism and my ability to demonstrate that all the areas which I was exploring were relevant to the Defence and he was allowing me to make my full and fair record, as I'm entitled to do so. I don't know if I'm answering Your Honour's question, but I think at some point you'll, at least in the beginning you'll have to take us at our word, and it's up to us to demonstrate to you and the rest of the Bench that we know what we're doing, we're prepared, we're not engaging in some fishing expedition, it's quite relevant, and we're actually trying to ask questions that are pertinent in not only exploring the truth but also assisting the Trial Chamber in making its findings of facts and conclusions of law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I appreciate what you have just said. You stressed one point in particular that seems fundamental to me. You explained that the questions you would put are there to help the Judges, and it is indeed an attitude that would be the attitude of everybody, be it in the examination-in-chief or in the cross-examination. You're not putting questions to please the witness or the people outside this courtroom. You put questions so that Judges may draw conclusions from what they hear. This, therefore, requires a professional attitude by everybody and a very clear objective, which is to inform the Judges of particular things. And I keep saying that. In your questions do endeavour to go to the core of the matter. Do not drown the witness in irrelevant questions. Well, sometimes you want to drown the Judges as well but, you know, if the Judge is a professional, he is never drowned in anything. You will see that early enough. I fully share what you have just said. You stressed the issue of the expert witnesses. Indeed, experience has shown us that when you have an expert witness, you also have a report, and the expert witness is examined-in-chief for an hour or two by the Prosecution on the main points in the report. Thereafter, the Defence will need much more time for its cross-examination. That's obvious. No problem regarding expert witnesses. But when it comes to factual witnesses who are going to speak to crimes allegedly committed in municipalities, whether they were victims or eyewitnesses to those facts, then fairness requires that if the Prosecution have two hours, there will be two hours for the Defence. But of course if there is another Defence counsel who wants another two hours, he must agree. So nothing else to say. No major objection to what you have just said at this stage. Of course I wish to know what the other Defence counsel think about it. Second Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Actually, I really have nothing to add what you said just now. I think that this is a principle which is perfectly valid. As far as these other witnesses are concerned, we will really try to have the Defence attorneys put questions that only have to do with their own clients. We're not going to waste time and I'm sure that we will be able to reach agreement on everything. It is a fact, of course, that sometimes more time will be required for cross-examination, perhaps of one single attorney in relation to the time that the Prosecutor had, but the Prosecutor gave us an approximation of the time required and perhaps he will not be able to abide by it all the time. Sometimes he will need less time; sometimes he will need more time. So if we want to conduct these proceedings in a serious and responsible manner, we as the Defence, too, if we put questions that can only be of assistance to the Court, then I believe that we can easily reach agreement with regard to every specific witness and every particular case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we've agreed on expert witnesses, where we should be relatively flexible in terms of the time required and to allow cross-examination to go on even longer than the direct examination, I believe that we should also reach agreement on other witnesses too. I believe that we should be very flexible in this regard as well. First of all, I think that it is unacceptable for the entire Defence to get the same amount of time as the Prosecution or, rather, I'm trying to say that the Defence should have considerably more time. I agree that this time should not be multiplied with the number six, that is to say the number of the accused. Perhaps it is possible to find a different reasonable figure, but at any rate, I believe there should be more time, manyfold at that. Whether we're going to use it every time or not depends on the circumstances involved. I'm sure we are not going to be putting questions that we do not consider relevant for our case and for the Court. So perhaps we should all give this some time, how much time this would actually be. But we should also bear flexibility in mind. If it would be expedient for these proceedings, then perhaps we should use even more time for examining some particular witnesses, so let us do it without a major problem. As for the order of questioning, I would agree with Mr. Karnavas on that. Regardless of the witness's particular testimony, we should take the witnesses in a set order. If we know that somebody has greater interest and a larger number of questions, then of course we will accommodate that person and leave them more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Valentin Coric subscribes to what our colleagues have said. We believe that setting a firm and definitive criterion would not be in the interests of a fair trial. We particularly subscribe to Mr. Karnavas's proposal, and supported by Ms. Alaburic, that we stick to the set order from the Prosecution and the indictment itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was in a case where there were two accused persons, and we used 50 per cent more time than the Prosecutor had for the direct examination. The situation is far more delicate here. There are six accused persons. And as the Defence counsel for Mr. Petkovic said, I believe that we should have the same amount of time but, on the other hand, it's not realistic if we all have the same amount of time. So we have to reduce this to a realistic framework, say two times more or three times more, what Mr. Karnavas elaborated on. First of all, not only in the question in respect of expert witnesses but lay witnesses as well, probably more time will be required, more time than used by the Prosecution. My experience before you, Mr. President, was very positive. We always found elegant solutions, if I may say so, and we always managed to deal with the questions in a way that would be of assistance to the Court and the interests of a fair trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I know that you would have liked to cross-examine yourself, but now you have a lawyer to represent you, so you will miss this opportunity. Nevertheless, I give you the floor in case you have something to say. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, while I had a lawyer, and I hope that I'm going to get Mr. Kovacic again and Mrs. Nika Pinter, I asked for myself to be given the right as well to cross-examine witnesses, in part, and this is why, sir: Until now, unfortunately, in many hearings before The Hague Tribunal some things were not treated the way they should be, in my judgement. Many facts important for understanding the events in the former Yugoslavia remained distorted to such a degree they led to total misinterpretation. I'm sorry to say, and perhaps it would not be a proper thing for me to say, but then I am an accused person here, I have been indicted: I have a degree in sociology, philosophy, electrical engineering, and I have other degrees, and I believe I'm intellectually capable of dealing with these matters, and I know about a great many things, even about things that professional lawyers don't know about, given their limited remit. If you look at my experience from 1968 onwards and in the war, I held about 15 important offices, and I believe that in the history of philosophy, in the sociology of war, the theory of war, the behaviour of a group in extreme and chaotic situations, in the spell of evil, the quantity of evil that appears in regulated states and also the discovered crimes in organised states, and if we look at the history of Croatia, I can give such relevant facts, and I can relevantly examine experts in particular. And, Your Honour, I'm going to ask for this to be made possible for me, parallel to my lawyers in some cases where I believe this would be a good thing, I would like to speak together with my lawyers and to put my own questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Praljak, I listened to you with great care. However, you raise a new problem there. You want to know whether, in spite of the Rules, an accused person may have, in addition to his lawyer, the right to put questions to a witness. Well, I'll think it over. So I believe you are making an oral application here which you have reasoned by saying that this is going to deal with political matters and that you have been involved in politics since 1968, so you are better able than your lawyer to put questions to an expert witness should this expert mention this type of question. Well, I'll think it over, as I said. I don't know what Mr. Prlic's lawyer feels about it, or the other lawyers, but I guess it's a question for them too. Quite a challenge. So this is on standby, as it were, for the time being, but there will be an answer. Turning to the Prosecution, do you have some light to shed on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure we can shed any light on it but let me try with a relatively small flashlight. I don't think at this point we can take this discussion much further, but let me just point out two other factors that we believe are important at this point. First of all, in the event that the Trial Chamber would like to hear arguments of the parties on the issue raised just now by Mr. Praljak, I can assure you that the Prosecution would like to be heard on that matter and our initial position would be that we do not believe it is permissible for an accused to cross-examine witnesses when that accused is represented by counsel, but we would certainly be -- like to be given an opportunity to fully brief and argue that matter in the event that the Trial Chamber or the Pre-Trial Judge thinks that would be helpful in order to advance that limited issue. And the final point I would like to put on the record at this point, Your Honour, again to go -- to take the issue of trial protocols kind of to an extreme, the Prosecution would point out that we do not believe that it is fair in a situation where we're given two hours to conduct a direct examination, for each of the six accused to be allotted two hours as well, thus meaning in effect there's 12 hours for the cumulative Defence teams whereby there would be obviously a high degree of overlap on many if not most of the issues that will be before Your Honours, and we would simply reiterate that we don't believe it's fair to have a system whereby we're allowed two hours for direct examination and the combined Defence teams are allowed 12 hours to cross-examine that same witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could just respond to a couple of points. First, I think Mr. Praljak's request is a reasonable one under certain circumstances, depending on the witness, and of course I noticed yesterday's order giving him counsel. What I didn't see in the order, and perhaps it wasn't necessary to do so, but it said counsel -- not counsel and co-counsel and also what comes with that, that is legal assistant, case manager, and what have you. So if Mr. Praljak were to receive, say, new counsel, of course I don't see how a new counsel would be able to articulate the thoughts and pose the sort of questions that Mr. Praljak has in mind, particularly given his level of experience and understanding, his background and his education. Number two, should he be given both of his prior counsel - and I strongly advise that, in the interests of justice, knowing both of them to be highly qualified, highly professional, and they do have an understanding of this case - that perhaps any of the questions that Mr. Praljak may need to ask could be asked through those lawyers, though there may be an exception on occasion. I don't think it needs to be the rule but an exceptional occasion could be made, but nonetheless if he has both of his counsel and a team as everybody else has, I don't see why perhaps his counsel would not be able to find the common ground with Mr. Praljak to pose those sort of questions. But again, if Mr. Praljak was not allowed to pose those questions, then I think we would have to find some sort of flexible approach in Court where counsel would be able to consult with the client during the questioning, and I would even advise, in support, that on -- depending on the type of witness, I would support an application for Mr. Praljak to be sitting actually next to his counsel as they would do, say, in the United States, or he could possibly write notes to his -- to his counsel. I just throw that out as an example and as something to think about. With respect to Mr. Mundis raised two times six equals 12, I don't think that anyone on this side of the table has actually promoted that concept, though I think the Trial Chamber was very clear that that is a possibility if we cannot find common ground. Again, I want to stress and repeat: We intend to ask questions that are relevant, consistent with our theories of the case, and again as you well noted, Your Honour, and as I pointed out, our purpose is here to assist you in finding a fair resolution for our clients. It makes no sense for me to be making political speeches. I'm not a cause-oriented lawyer. My cause is my client and his case based on the indictment that was drafted by the Prosecution. So I don't think the Prosecutors need worry that we're asking for two times six equals 12. However, there may be instances where we're going to need to be a little bit flexible and what I'm not hearing anything from that side of the table is that they have any predisposition against flexibility. In fact, I hear the opposite and that's a welcoming sign, particularly given that today we've had some rather difficult moments in the court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On that issue I would like to invite the Prosecution and the Defence to meet up and in order to suggest to me a modus operandi in due course in order for the proceedings to run smoothly. The flexibility approach seems to me to be the right one in order to find the right way to proceed with each witness on a case-by-case basis. Regarding the issues raised by Mr. Praljak, of course we will need to examine the matter very thoroughly. I will consider the matter, and I will probably issue an order in due course in order to ask you to make submissions on both sides, to make submissions on that point, because it seems to me that this is a vital issue when it comes to the rights of the accused. We still have 20 minutes to go. We still have a lot of items on the agenda. Let me move to the disclosure of evidence pursuant to Rule 66 and 68. I'd like to turn to the Prosecution. Can you tell us where we stand on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we -- just last week I believe there was further disclosure in this case. Disclosure, as Your Honour is well aware, is ongoing, and we are continuing to take steps to ensure that all disclosure-related issues are resolved as quickly as possible and certainly prior to the trial with respect, obviously, to Rule 66 material, and of course Rule 68 is an ongoing obligation of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be heard, Your Honour. And again I appreciate the time that you're giving me. One, I don't believe we have a lot of the expert reports. Perhaps they are hidden in that EDS system, which is not the most user-friendly. However, I believe we do have some reports that are missing. And speaking of expert reports, I am aware of one preliminary report that was prepared by an expert with respect to a very important issue which I believe is important to all of the accused, and that is the Mujahedin that were operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So a preliminary report was presented by the expert to the OTP. I have made requests of that report. I haven't received it. Of course, this is an outside expert, and I make that distinction. In-house meaning that you can -- you know, there's a difference when somebody is an employee called. An analyst writes a report and then of course you can sit around and sort of feather it, polish it and what have you, versus an outside. And of course, given that there is preliminary report, barring any additional evidence, I certainly would like to have each and every one of these preliminary reports to see in the event a particular report may take a southern or northern turn, as it were. So if at all possible, I would request that these sorts of reports also be provided to us, including the one that I'm referencing which members of the OTP are aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If the other counsel do not have anything specific to add on that particular issue, I'd like to move on to something else. Earlier on the Defence mentioned the financial issue. Do you want to deal with that in open session or in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think Your Honour, for the sake of transparency, I think it's best to deal with it in open session. I've had conversations with the -- with the Registry already. I've already contacted them and I've already informed them that I would be mentioning this on the record in public because I do think there is a certain transparency that's required. As of February, it has become very clear that for this particular Defence team, Defence counsel, lead counsel, will have to, one, forego any income and in fact have to spend money already earned which has yet to be delivered by the Registry in financing the rest of the team. Now, there was one particular issue with respect to the previous counsel. Money was not provided to us for a certain -- for phase 2, primarily because that counsel was not on Rule 45. However, the Registry was imminently informed as to the status of the case when I received it, and the amount of work that I had to deal with in part covered all of the work that would have been done or should have been done on phase 2. Nevertheless, we were derived of those funds and I've had to make do. The case was scheduled originally to start in October, then they talked about November, December, and then in February. Eventually it was settled on a breakdown of February, with 20 per cent being withheld. That 20 per cent, of course, being lead counsel, it is my practice to make sure that everybody in the staff gets paid first, and what -- if there is anything left, then it's for counsel, as opposed to doing it the other way around. And I want to stress so that the Trial Chamber understands, which I'm sure it does understand, that behind any face that works on the Defence team, there are other faces, there are other people, be they husbands, wives, mothers, children. So it's not just a particular individual but it's their families and loved ones that also rely on the income. So obviously, for those reasons, I make sure that they get paid first. So the 20 per cent, of course, was withheld up until February. Now, for reasons that are beyond the control of this particular Defence team, or any Defence team, and in fact I would lay the blame squarely on the Registry to some extent because it is they who are responsible for making sure that this building is up to snuff, and if it needs to be refurbished, it should be refurbished in a timely fashion, but the trial is being continued, as I understand it, from February to perhaps April in part, or primarily because of the lack of courtroom space. I can understand that. What needs to be understood, however, is that throughout this period from February, beginning of February all the way until the beginning of the trial, the Prosecution continues to work on the case, they continue to investigate the case, the case grows bigger and bigger. They're entitled to do that. That's their mandate. Nothing prevents them, there's no dossier, and I think that they would not be doing their duty if they did not continue to investigate and prepare their case. On the other hand -- and I want to also stress that when Mr. Scott earlier was addressing the Court he had indicated all the efforts that he was making in trying to get everything ready as the Court had indicated, and in fact, Your Honour, you indicated that you had been working close to 24 hours a day. Suffice it to say those of us who have practiced on the Defence side knows that as the case becomes gets closer and close to trial, one needs to work harder and harder. Unfortunately, I've had to lay off staff. I've had to reduce hours just to make sure that the money was stretched enough. I'm mentioning this not because I'm asking at this point in time for Court intervention, but merely to state what I've stated to the Registry, that should there come a time at the end of this month where we cannot find some sort of a reasonable resolution -- and what I'm asking for is the allotment that would be normally due to a case of this magnitude, keeping in mind that by the time the trial begins I would have been in case for 16 or 17 months, that it be given, because of these extraordinary circumstances and because I'm trying to do my job. I'm responsible for the life of an individual. That's what it comes down to when you are a Defence lawyer. I'm responsible to make sure that he gets a fair trial. I have certain professional responsibilities. Now, in meeting those responsibilities, I understand that I must put his interests up first. I've done that in my entire career. However, there comes a time also where I have to take a principle position, and that is do I work for free for the United Nations and subsidise this Tribunal because it wishes to prosecute somebody but then at the same time does not wish to provide sufficient funds to allow that individual to have a full and fair Defence? So I bring this to your attention because I've also notified the Registry that there may come a time where I will have to make a rather difficult choice, and the choice may be to lay off the entire team until the beginning of the trial, or to finance -- continue to finance the defence of Mr. Prlic until the beginning of the trial. Now, I'm told not to worry, that once the trial begins I can begin getting paid. I want to remind those who work in the Registry that we don't get hospitalisation, we don't get benefits, we're not on some UN pension, we certainly don't get the six-weeks paid vacations. And so -- and we have a tremendous amount of overhead, particularly if an individual is out on provisional release where you do have to have contact with that individual, and here in this particular case we're talking about a document case as opposed to a witness case. There lies the difference. And who better than your own client to assist you in sifting through these documents? So because of that we've had to -- I have had to more or less move to Croatia, work in Bosnia, while at the same time maintain premises here, ready for trial, and I was prepared to start trial in October, as I thought we would. So I mention this on the record because there may come a time where I will either ask for intervention or at least put the Trial Chamber on notice that I will need an order from the Trial Chamber directing me to work for free for the UN as if I were some indentured servant. That's what it will take, because I think that it's unbecoming to expect Defence counsel who are trying to do a reasonable job in protecting their client's rights to actually finance their cases when there are alternative ways. And in this particular case, the phase 2 money was withheld from us to no fault of our own, to no fault of the client. The money is not going to the previous counsel, it's not going to work that was previously done but, rather, it's going for the next three months, which is not even sufficient but at least it would go for the next three months to pay for the staff to continue to work and for us to meet our professional and ethical responsibilities, and that's what I wanted to say, Your Honour, and I apologise for having to take up your time on this matter, but ultimately you are -- you are here to make sure and to guarantee the rights of the accused and make sure that their fundamental rights are protected, and it would be in the interests of justice, in my belief, if at least some flexibility was shown to at least provide us with the full amount that is allocated for these sorts of cases. Even though that's not sufficient, I'm not asking for anything more than that. I'm asking basically to have what all the other teams have in order to get their cases ready. Thank you, and again I apologise for taking everyone's time, including the Prosecutor's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for these comments, for this information. I will ask to meet with the Registrar in order to shed some light on this matter and in order to encourage him to solve this issue, because this problem should not exist. According to me, it's absolutely normal that assigned counsel should be paid for their work without any problems. I'll deal with it. I'm not going to give the floor to the other Defence counsel who I'm sure share what you've just said. We only have a few minutes left, and we'll move into private session. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. And let me state that the hearing stands adjourned, and we'll meet again very shortly.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at 1.48 p.m.
